items.question: How often should I water a Monstera deliciosa during active summer growth?
expected_facts: let the top inch or two of soil dry out before watering again
items.answer_text: Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering.
cited_quotes: Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. Let the Monstera drain fully after watering and never leave the pot sitting in standing water. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Drooping or yellowing lower leaves on a Monstera frequently signal overwatering rather than thirst, so check the soil before adding more water.

Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. Brown, crispy leaf edges on a Monstera usually indicate low humidity or underwatering, and raising humidity to around 60 percent can help. Few or no leaf splits on a younger Monstera are normal, and fenestration typically increases as the plant matures and receives brighter light. Pests such as spider mites and mealybugs sometimes appear on a Monstera, and wiping the leaves and treating with insecticidal soap usually controls them.

La Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta durante unas 6 a 8 horas al día. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar las hojas de una Monstera y dejar manchas pálidas o marrones, así que filtra la luz intensa con una cortina fina. Una Monstera mantenida en sombra profunda tiende a producir hojas más pequeñas y con menos de los característicos cortes y agujeros. Girar la Monstera un cuarto de vuelta cada semana le ayuda a crecer de forma uniforme hacia la fuente de luz.

The Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) grows best in bright, indirect light for roughly 6 to 8 hours a day. Direct midday sun can scorch the leaves of a Monstera, leaving pale or brown patches, so filter strong light through a sheer curtain. A Monstera kept in deep shade tends to produce smaller leaves with fewer of the characteristic splits and holes. Rotating the Monstera a quarter turn each week helps it grow evenly toward the light source.

Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. Brown, crispy leaf edges on a Monstera usually indicate low humidity or underwatering, and raising humidity to around 60 percent can help. Few or no leaf splits on a younger Monstera are normal, and fenestration typically increases as the plant matures and receives brighter light. Pests such as spider mites and mealybugs sometimes appear on a Monstera, and wiping the leaves and treating with insecticidal soap usually controls them.

La referencia citada incluye la Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) como tóxica para gatos y perros; la ingestión puede causar irritación bucal, ardor intenso de la boca y los labios, salivación excesiva, vómitos y dificultad para tragar. Estos efectos en la Monstera se deben a los cristales insolubles de oxalato de calcio presentes en las hojas y los tallos de la planta. Si un gato o un perro mastica cualquier parte de una Monstera, comunícate de inmediato con un veterinario o una línea de control de intoxicaciones de animales. Mantén la Monstera fuera del alcance de mascotas y niños para reducir la posibilidad de ingestión accidental.

Plant the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) in a loose, well-draining potting mix amended with bark, perlite, or coir to keep roots aerated. Choose a pot for the Monstera that has drainage holes and is only 2 to 5 centimeters wider than the current root ball. Repot the Monstera every 1 to 2 years in spring when roots begin circling the pot or emerging from the drainage holes. A mature Monstera benefits from a moss pole or stake, because its aerial roots will climb and support larger, more fenestrated leaves.

items.question: What kind of light does a Pothos prefer indoors?
items.answer_text: Leggy, sparse growth on a Pothos points to insufficient light, and moving it to a brighter spot encourages fuller foliage. Wiping the leaves of a Pothos occasionally removes dust and helps the plant absorb more light. Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) grows best in bright, indirect light and keeps its variegation strongest under those conditions.
cited_quotes: Yellowing leaves on a Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) are most commonly caused by overwatering or poor drainage. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a Pothos usually indicate underwatering, low humidity, or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Pothos can attract pests such as spider mites, mealybugs, and scale, which appear as fine webbing, white cottony spots, or small bumps on stems. Leggy, sparse growth on a Pothos points to insufficient light, and moving it to a brighter spot encourages fuller foliage. Wiping the leaves of a Pothos occasionally removes dust and helps the plant absorb more light.

Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) grows best in bright, indirect light and keeps its variegation strongest under those conditions. A Pothos will survive in low light, but its leaves turn more solidly green and the stems grow leggy with wider gaps between leaves. Direct midday sun can scorch a Pothos, leaving pale or bleached patches on the foliage. If a Pothos loses its yellow or white markings, moving it closer to a bright window usually restores the pattern over several weeks. Pothos does well a few feet from an east- or north-facing window.

Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) thrives in a loose, well-draining potting mix and dislikes dense soil that holds water around the roots. A blend of standard potting soil with added perlite or orchid bark gives Pothos the aeration it prefers. Repot a Pothos every one to two years, or when roots begin circling the pot or pushing through the drainage holes. When repotting Pothos, choose a container only one to two inches wider than the current one to avoid oversized pots that stay wet. A pot with drainage holes is important for Pothos because trapped moisture leads to root rot.

El Potho (Epipremnum aureum) crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta y mantiene su variegación más intensa en esas condiciones. Un Potho sobrevivirá con poca luz, pero sus hojas se vuelven de un verde más uniforme y los tallos se alargan con mayores espacios entre las hojas. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar un Potho y dejar manchas pálidas o decoloradas en el follaje. Si un Potho pierde sus marcas amarillas o blancas, acercarlo a una ventana luminosa suele restaurar el patrón a lo largo de varias semanas. El Potho se desarrolla bien a un par de pies de una ventana orientada al este o al norte.

Water Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) when the top inch of soil has dried out, which is usually every seven to ten days in spring and summer. In winter, Pothos needs water less often, roughly every fourteen to twenty-one days, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Pothos prefers to be watered thoroughly until liquid drains from the bottom, and then it should not sit in standing water. Drooping, soft leaves on a Pothos often signal overwatering, while crispy edges suggest the plant has stayed dry too long. A Pothos tolerates occasional missed waterings better than constantly soggy soil.

Las hojas amarillentas en un Potho (Epipremnum aureum) se deben con mayor frecuencia al exceso de riego o al drenaje deficiente. Las puntas de las hojas marrones y secas en un Potho suelen indicar falta de riego, baja humedad o acumulación de sales minerales del agua del grifo. El Potho puede atraer plagas como ácaros, cochinillas algodonosas y cochinillas con caparazón, que aparecen como telarañas finas, manchas blancas algodonosas o pequeños bultos en los tallos. El crecimiento alargado y escaso en un Potho indica luz insuficiente, y trasladarlo a un lugar más brillante favorece un follaje más tupido. Limpiar las hojas del Potho de vez en cuando elimina el polvo y ayuda a la planta a absorber más luz.

items.question: Why does a snake plant rot so easily if I water it too much?
items.answer_text: In winter, snake plant needs water much less often, roughly once every four to six weeks. Always empty the saucer after watering snake plant, because standing water rots its rhizomes. If the leaves of a snake plant turn soft, mushy, or yellow at the base, the most common cause is too much water.

In winter, snake plant needs water much less often, roughly once every four to six weeks. Always empty the saucer after watering snake plant, because standing water rots its rhizomes. If the leaves of a snake plant turn soft, mushy, or yellow at the base, the most common cause is too much water.

retrieved_contexts.text: Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) stores water in its thick upright leaves and tolerates infrequent watering far better than overwatering. Water snake plant only when the top two inches of soil have dried completely, which is often every two to three weeks in summer. In winter, snake plant needs water much less often, roughly once every four to six weeks. Always empty the saucer after watering snake plant, because standing water rots its rhizomes. If the leaves of a snake plant turn soft, mushy, or yellow at the base, the most common cause is too much water.

The most frequent problem with snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) is root rot caused by overwatering, which shows as soft, yellowing, or collapsing leaves. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a snake plant often follow underwatering or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Wrinkled or curling leaves signal that the snake plant is too dry and needs a thorough watering. Cold drafts below 50 degrees Fahrenheit can leave pale scarred patches on snake plant leaves. If a snake plant is not growing, move it to brighter indirect light and resume regular feeding during the growing season.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand. Plant snake plant in a pot with drainage holes, because the rhizomes are prone to rot in waterlogged soil. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years. Repot snake plant in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. Terracotta pots suit snake plant well because the porous clay wicks away excess moisture.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) adapts to a wide range of light, from bright indirect sun to fairly dim corners. The strongest growth and the boldest leaf banding on a snake plant appear in bright, indirect light. A snake plant kept in deep shade survives but grows slowly and produces thinner leaves. Protect snake plant from prolonged direct midday sun through glass, which can scorch and bleach the leaves. Rotating the snake plant a quarter turn every few weeks keeps its upright leaves growing evenly.

The cited reference lists snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, and nausea. The compounds responsible in snake plant are saponins, which irritate the mouth and digestive tract of pets. Keep snake plant out of reach of cats and dogs, and place it where a curious pet cannot chew the leaves. If a cat or dog has eaten any part of a snake plant, contact a veterinarian or an animal poison-control line. The cited reference describes the snake plant reaction as generally mild to moderate, but a professional should still evaluate the animal.

La lengua de suegra (Dracaena trifasciata) necesita una mezcla de drenaje rápido, como un sustrato para cactus y suculentas combinado con perlita adicional o arena gruesa. Planta la lengua de suegra en una maceta con orificios de drenaje, porque los rizomas tienden a pudrirse en sustrato encharcado. La lengua de suegra prefiere estar ligeramente apretada en su maceta y solo necesita trasplante cada tres o cuatro años. Trasplanta la lengua de suegra en primavera, pasándola a un recipiente solo una talla más grande. Las macetas de terracota le van bien a la lengua de suegra porque la arcilla porosa absorbe el exceso de humedad.

items.question: Why are my peace lily's leaves drooping, and will it recover after watering?
expected_facts: drooping leaves often signal the plant needs water
items.answer_text: The Peace lily wilts visibly when it is thirsty, and it usually recovers within a few hours of a thorough watering. Use room-temperature water and empty the saucer after watering the Peace lily. Yellowing leaves on the Peace lily usually point to overwatering or roots that have been sitting in water too long.
cited_quotes: Water the Peace lily when the top inch of soil feels dry to the touch, which is roughly once every five to seven days in warm months. The Peace lily wilts visibly when it is thirsty, and it usually recovers within a few hours of a thorough watering. Reduce watering for the Peace lily in winter to about once every ten to fourteen days, because the plant grows slowly and the soil stays wet longer. Always let excess water drain away, since the Peace lily is prone to root rot if its roots sit in standing water. Use room-temperature water and empty the saucer after watering the Peace lily.

Brown leaf tips on a Peace lily often signal low humidity, mineral buildup from tap water, or over-fertilizing. Yellowing leaves on the Peace lily usually point to overwatering or roots that have been sitting in water too long. If the Peace lily droops dramatically, check the soil first, as both underwatering and severe overwatering can cause wilting. Few or no flowers on the Peace lily commonly mean the light is too low or the plant is too young to bloom. Wipe the broad leaves of the Peace lily occasionally to remove dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and mealybugs.

Always let excess water drain away, since the Peace lily is prone to root rot if its roots sit in standing water. Use room-temperature water and empty the saucer after watering the Peace lily.

Brown leaf tips on a Peace lily often signal low humidity, mineral buildup from tap water, or over-fertilizing. Yellowing leaves on the Peace lily usually point to overwatering or roots that have been sitting in water too long. If the Peace lily droops dramatically, check the soil first, as both underwatering and severe overwatering can cause wilting. Few or no flowers on the Peace lily commonly mean the light is too low or the plant is too young to bloom. Wipe the broad leaves of the Peace lily occasionally to remove dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and mealybugs.

The cited reference lists Peace lily (Spathiphyllum) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, intense burning of the mouth and lips, drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. Keep the Peace lily out of direct midday sun, because hot direct rays can scorch its leaves and leave brown patches. A spot a few feet back from an east- or north-facing window suits the Peace lily well. In very low light the Peace lily will survive but it may stop producing its white flowering spathes. If the Peace lily's leaves look pale or leggy, move it to a brighter location with filtered light.

Choose a pot with drainage holes, because the Peace lily will not tolerate waterlogged soil. Repot the Peace lily every one to two years in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. items.answer_text: A healthy Spider plant produces baby plantlets on long stems, and these can be rooted in water or soil to grow new plants. The Spider plant tolerates moderate to low light, though variegation fades and new plantlets form more slowly in dim conditions.

The Spider plant can attract spider mites and aphids in dry indoor air, so inspect the undersides of leaves and wipe them down regularly. A healthy Spider plant produces baby plantlets on long stems, and these can be rooted in water or soil to grow new plants.

The Spider plant grows best in bright, indirect light near an east- or north-facing window. Direct midday sun can scorch the foliage, so keep the Spider plant out of harsh, unfiltered beams. items.question: Why is my fiddle-leaf fig dropping leaves after I moved it to a new room?
expected_facts: sensitive to sudden changes in light or location
items.answer_text: Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. In low light the Fiddle-leaf fig grows slowly, drops lower leaves, and may lean toward the brightest part of the room. Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves.
cited_quotes: Brown spots on a Fiddle-leaf fig often signal overwatering or root rot, especially when the spots start at the leaf edges and the soil stays wet. Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. Pale or yellowing lower leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig can point to too little light or a nutrient shortage during active growth. Wipe the broad leaves of the Fiddle-leaf fig with a damp cloth now and then to clear dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and scale. Steady light, steady watering, and stable temperature prevent most Fiddle-leaf fig problems.

The Fiddle-leaf fig prefers bright, indirect light and does best near an east- or south-facing window with a sheer curtain. A few hours of gentle morning sun suit the Fiddle-leaf fig, but harsh midday sun through glass can scorch its large leaves. In low light the Fiddle-leaf fig grows slowly, drops lower leaves, and may lean toward the brightest part of the room. Rotate the Fiddle-leaf fig a quarter turn every week or two so the plant grows evenly on all sides. Keep the Fiddle-leaf fig away from cold drafts and heating vents, which stress the foliage.

Water your Fiddle-leaf fig when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in the growing season. Always water the Fiddle-leaf fig thoroughly until liquid drains from the pot, then discard whatever collects in the saucer. Reduce watering for the Fiddle-leaf fig in winter, when the plant uses less moisture and the soil stays damp longer. Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves. Let the moisture level guide your schedule rather than watering on a fixed calendar day.

El exceso de riego es la causa más común de fracaso con el Aloe vera, así que ante la duda, espera unos días más antes de regar.

Soft, mushy, or translucent leaves on an Aloe vera usually signal overwatering and the onset of root rot. Thin, curling leaves instead point to underwatering, so check whether the Aloe vera has gone too long without a drink. Brown, crispy leaf tips on Aloe vera can follow sudden exposure to intense direct sun before the plant has acclimated. A pale, stretched, and floppy Aloe vera is reaching for more light and should be moved gradually to a brighter location. If the base of the Aloe vera turns dark and soft, remove the plant, cut away rotted tissue, and repot it in fresh dry succulent mix.

Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) is a succulent that stores water in its leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water Aloe vera deeply but infrequently, allowing the top two inches of soil to become completely dry first. In spring and summer this usually means watering Aloe vera about every two to three weeks, while in winter the interval often stretches to once a month or less. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure with Aloe vera, so when in doubt, wait a few more days before watering. Always discard any water that collects in the saucer so that the roots of your Aloe vera never sit in moisture.

Aloe vera grows best in bright light and tolerates several hours of direct sun once acclimated. Place Aloe vera near a south- or west-facing window where it receives at least six hours of strong light each day. A plant kept in low light will stretch and grow pale, so move a leggy Aloe vera gradually toward a brighter spot to avoid leaf scorch. If you move Aloe vera outdoors for summer, increase sun exposure slowly over one to two weeks. Leaves that turn reddish-brown often indicate that the Aloe vera is receiving more intense sun than it has adjusted to.

El Aloe vera necesita una mezcla de drenaje rápido, así que usa un sustrato para cactus o suculentas enriquecido con perlita adicional o arena gruesa. Trasplanta el Aloe vera cada dos o tres años, o antes cuando los hijuelos llenen la maceta o las raíces asomen por los orificios de drenaje. Elige una maceta solo una talla más grande, porque un recipiente demasiado grande retiene exceso de humedad alrededor de las raíces del Aloe vera. Después del trasplante, espera alrededor de una semana antes de regar el Aloe vera para que las raíces removidas puedan cicatrizar.

items.question: Why do my Calathea leaves curl and get crispy edges?
expected_facts: sensitive to low humidity and to minerals in tap water
items.answer_text: Crispy brown leaf edges on a Calathea usually signal low humidity, mineral-heavy water, or letting the soil dry out too far. Calathea prefers consistently moist soil and reacts to drought by curling and crisping its leaf edges. Yellowing lower leaves on the Calathea often point to overwatering or a pot that drains poorly, so check that the mix is not staying waterlogged.
cited_quotes: Crispy brown leaf edges on a Calathea usually signal low humidity, mineral-heavy water, or letting the soil dry out too far. Raise the humidity around your Calathea to roughly 50 to 60 percent with a pebble tray or a nearby humidifier. Yellowing lower leaves on the Calathea often point to overwatering or a pot that drains poorly, so check that the mix is not staying waterlogged. If the Calathea stops folding its leaves upward at night, it may be receiving too little light or too much stress from inconsistent watering. Spider mites can attack a stressed Calathea, so inspect the undersides of the leaves and rinse them if you spot fine webbing.

Water your Calathea when the top inch of the potting mix has begun to dry, which is often about once every five to seven days in the growing season. Calathea prefers consistently moist soil and reacts to drought by curling and crisping its leaf edges. This plant is sensitive to mineral buildup, so water your Calathea with filtered, distilled, or rested rainwater rather than hard tap water. Reduce watering for the Calathea in winter to roughly every ten to fourteen days, letting the surface dry slightly more between drinks. Never let the Calathea sit in a saucer of standing water, because soggy roots lead to rot.

items.question: Why is my Dracaena getting brown leaf tips?
expected_facts: brown tips often from fluoride or salts in tap water
items.answer_text: Brown leaf tips on Dracaena (Dracaena) usually point to fluoride in tap water, underwatering, or low humidity. Dracaena can develop brown leaf tips when watered with fluoride- or chlorine-heavy tap water, so use filtered or distilled water if tips brown.
cited_quotes: Brown leaf tips on Dracaena (Dracaena) usually point to fluoride in tap water, underwatering, or low humidity. Yellowing lower leaves on Dracaena are often a normal sign of aging, but widespread yellowing can indicate overwatering. Drooping or soft stems on Dracaena typically signal soggy soil and the early stages of root rot, so check that the mix drains freely. Pale or stretched growth on Dracaena means it is not receiving enough light and should be moved closer to a window. Inspect Dracaena regularly for spider mites and mealybugs, which can appear in dry indoor air and are treated by wiping the leaves and applying insecticidal soap.

Water Dracaena (Dracaena) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is usually every 7 to 10 days in active growth. Dracaena is sensitive to overwatering, so let excess water drain fully and never leave the pot sitting in a saucer of water. In winter, reduce watering for Dracaena to roughly every 14 to 21 days because the plant uses less water in cooler, lower-light conditions. Dracaena can develop brown leaf tips when watered with fluoride- or chlorine-heavy tap water, so use filtered or distilled water if tips brown. Water Dracaena until a little moisture escapes the drainage holes, then discard whatever collects beneath the pot.

items.question: How often should I water a jade plant, and what soil does it need?
expected_facts: water sparingly and use a well-draining succulent mix
items.answer_text: Water the Jade plant deeply, then let the top two-thirds of the soil dry before watering again. In spring and summer the Jade plant may need water roughly every two to three weeks, while in winter it may need water only once a month. Wrinkled or shriveled leaves on the Jade plant indicate it is too dry and needs a thorough watering.
cited_quotes: The Jade plant (Crassula ovata) stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water the Jade plant deeply, then let the top two-thirds of the soil dry before watering again. In spring and summer the Jade plant may need water roughly every two to three weeks, while in winter it may need water only once a month. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure with the Jade plant, so err toward keeping it dry. Always empty the saucer so the Jade plant never sits in standing water.

Soft, mushy, or yellowing leaves on the Jade plant usually signal overwatering or poor drainage. Wrinkled or shriveled leaves on the Jade plant indicate it is too dry and needs a thorough watering. Leaf drop on the Jade plant can follow sudden temperature swings, cold drafts, or moving it abruptly into harsh sun. Mealybugs sometimes appear in the leaf joints of the Jade plant and can be wiped away with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol. Keep the Jade plant above 50 degrees Fahrenheit, since it is sensitive to frost.

items.question: Why does my Boston fern keep getting dry, brown fronds in my heated apartment?
expected_facts: needs consistently high humidity and evenly moist soil
items.answer_text: Because the Boston fern resents dry air, mist its fronds or set the pot on a humidity tray to keep relative humidity near 50 to 70 percent. Browning frond tips on the Boston fern usually signal low humidity, underwatering, or excess fertilizer salts in the soil. Allowing the Boston fern to dry out completely will cause the delicate leaflets to brown and drop.
cited_quotes: The Boston fern prefers soil that stays evenly and consistently moist but never waterlogged. Water the Boston fern whenever the top half inch of the potting mix begins to feel dry to the touch. In a warm, well-lit room the Boston fern often needs watering two or three times per week, while in winter once every five to seven days is usually enough. Because the Boston fern resents dry air, mist its fronds or set the pot on a humidity tray to keep relative humidity near 50 to 70 percent. Allowing the Boston fern to dry out completely will cause the delicate leaflets to brown and drop.

Browning frond tips on the Boston fern usually signal low humidity, underwatering, or excess fertilizer salts in the soil. Yellowing fronds across the Boston fern often point to overwatering or poor drainage at the roots. If the Boston fern sheds many leaflets indoors, the most common cause is dry air combined with inconsistent watering. Inspect the Boston fern for scale insects and spider mites, which appear when the air is too dry and warm. Trimming dead fronds at the base helps the Boston fern channel energy into healthy new growth.

items.question: How do I get my Phalaenopsis orchid to rebloom after the flowers drop?
expected_facts: cut back the spent flower spike and provide a slight nighttime temperature drop
items.answer_text: Bud blast, where flower buds yellow and drop before opening, happens when the Orchid faces drafts, sudden temperature swings, or dry air. If the Orchid stops blooming, a drop in night temperature of about ten degrees Fahrenheit for a few weeks often triggers a new flower spike. Repot the Orchid every one to two years, ideally just after flowering finishes, to refresh the bark before it breaks down and suffocates the roots.
cited_quotes: The most common problem with the Orchid (Phalaenopsis) is root rot from soggy bark, shown by mushy brown roots and wilting leaves. Wrinkled, leathery leaves on the Orchid usually mean underwatering or dehydrated roots rather than too much water. Bud blast, where flower buds yellow and drop before opening, happens when the Orchid faces drafts, sudden temperature swings, or dry air. Sticky residue or small white cottony spots can indicate mealybugs or scale on the Orchid, which you can wipe off with a cotton swab dipped in diluted alcohol. If the Orchid stops blooming, a drop in night temperature of about ten degrees Fahrenheit for a few weeks often triggers a new flower spike.

Pot the Orchid (Phalaenopsis) in a coarse, free-draining medium such as graded fir bark rather than ordinary houseplant soil. Repot the Orchid every one to two years, ideally just after flowering finishes, to refresh the bark before it breaks down and suffocates the roots. Choose a clear or slotted pot so you can see the Orchid's roots and check moisture at a glance. When repotting, trim away any soft, brown, or hollow roots and keep the firm pale ones. A pot only slightly larger than the old one keeps the Orchid from staying too wet.

items.question: Why are the lower leaves on my Monstera deliciosa turning yellow?
items.answer_text: Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. Drooping or yellowing lower leaves on a Monstera frequently signal overwatering rather than thirst, so check the soil before adding more water. The Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) grows best in bright, indirect light for roughly 6 to 8 hours a day.
cited_quotes: Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. Brown, crispy leaf edges on a Monstera usually indicate low humidity or underwatering, and raising humidity to around 60 percent can help. Few or no leaf splits on a younger Monstera are normal, and fenestration typically increases as the plant matures and receives brighter light. Pests such as spider mites and mealybugs sometimes appear on a Monstera, and wiping the leaves and treating with insecticidal soap usually controls them.

Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. Let the Monstera drain fully after watering and never leave the pot sitting in standing water. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Drooping or yellowing lower leaves on a Monstera frequently signal overwatering rather than thirst, so check the soil before adding more water.

The Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) grows best in bright, indirect light for roughly 6 to 8 hours a day. Direct midday sun can scorch the leaves of a Monstera, leaving pale or brown patches, so filter strong light through a sheer curtain. A Monstera kept in deep shade tends to produce smaller leaves with fewer of the characteristic splits and holes. Rotating the Monstera a quarter turn each week helps it grow evenly toward the light source.

Direct midday sun can scorch a Pothos, leaving pale or bleached patches on the foliage. If a Pothos loses its yellow or white markings, moving it closer to a bright window usually restores the pattern over several weeks. Pothos does well a few feet from an east- or north-facing window.

items.question: What light conditions does a snake plant need?
items.answer_text: Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years. Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) adapts to a wide range of light, from bright indirect sun to fairly dim corners.
cited_quotes: Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand. Plant snake plant in a pot with drainage holes, because the rhizomes are prone to rot in waterlogged soil. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years. Repot snake plant in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. Terracotta pots suit snake plant well because the porous clay wicks away excess moisture.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) adapts to a wide range of light, from bright indirect sun to fairly dim corners. The strongest growth and the boldest leaf banding on a snake plant appear in bright, indirect light. A snake plant kept in deep shade survives but grows slowly and produces thinner leaves. Protect snake plant from prolonged direct midday sun through glass, which can scorch and bleach the leaves. Rotating the snake plant a quarter turn every few weeks keeps its upright leaves growing evenly.

items.question: My peace lily is drooping and wilting, what does that mean?
items.answer_text: If the Peace lily droops dramatically, check the soil first, as both underwatering and severe overwatering can cause wilting. Few or no flowers on the Peace lily commonly mean the light is too low or the plant is too young to bloom. The Peace lily wilts visibly when it is thirsty, and it usually recovers within a few hours of a thorough watering.
cited_quotes: Brown leaf tips on a Peace lily often signal low humidity, mineral buildup from tap water, or over-fertilizing. Yellowing leaves on the Peace lily usually point to overwatering or roots that have been sitting in water too long. If the Peace lily droops dramatically, check the soil first, as both underwatering and severe overwatering can cause wilting. Few or no flowers on the Peace lily commonly mean the light is too low or the plant is too young to bloom. Wipe the broad leaves of the Peace lily occasionally to remove dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and mealybugs.

Water the Peace lily when the top inch of soil feels dry to the touch, which is roughly once every five to seven days in warm months. The Peace lily wilts visibly when it is thirsty, and it usually recovers within a few hours of a thorough watering. Reduce watering for the Peace lily in winter to about once every ten to fourteen days, because the plant grows slowly and the soil stays wet longer. Always let excess water drain away, since the Peace lily is prone to root rot if its roots sit in standing water. Use room-temperature water and empty the saucer after watering the Peace lily.

items.question: Why is my fiddle-leaf fig dropping leaves?

Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves. items.question: How often should I water my aloe vera?
items.answer_text: In spring and summer this usually means watering Aloe vera about every two to three weeks, while in winter the interval often stretches to once a month or less. Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) is a succulent that stores water in its leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water Aloe vera deeply but infrequently, allowing the top two inches of soil to become completely dry first.

Overwatering is the most common cause of failure with Aloe vera, so when in doubt, wait a few more days before watering. Always discard any water that collects in the saucer so that the roots of your Aloe vera never sit in moisture.

After repotting, wait about a week before watering the Aloe vera so that any disturbed roots can heal.

Aloe vera grows best in bright light and tolerates several hours of direct sun once acclimated. Leaves that turn reddish-brown often indicate that the Aloe vera is receiving more intense sun than it has adjusted to.

Soft, mushy, or translucent leaves on an Aloe vera usually signal overwatering and the onset of root rot. Thin, curling leaves instead point to underwatering, so check whether the Aloe vera has gone too long without a drink. Brown, crispy leaf tips on Aloe vera can follow sudden exposure to intense direct sun before the plant has acclimated. A pale, stretched, and floppy Aloe vera is reaching for more light and should be moved gradually to a brighter location. If the base of the Aloe vera turns dark and soft, remove the plant, cut away rotted tissue, and repot it in fresh dry succulent mix.

items.answer_text: Spring is the preferred time to repot the Rubber plant, as it recovers fastest during active growth. The Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) does best in a well-draining potting mix, such as a general houseplant mix amended with perlite or bark. A pot with drainage holes is important for the Rubber plant because the roots will rot in soil that stays saturated.
cited_quotes: The Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) does best in a well-draining potting mix, such as a general houseplant mix amended with perlite or bark. A pot with drainage holes is important for the Rubber plant because the roots will rot in soil that stays saturated. The Rubber plant is typically repotted every two to three years, or when roots begin circling the pot or emerging from the drainage holes. When repotting the Rubber plant, choose a container only one size larger to avoid leaving excess wet soil around the roots. Spring is the preferred time to repot the Rubber plant, as it recovers fastest during active growth.

items.question: How often should I water a jade plant?
expected_facts: allow the soil to dry between waterings
items.answer_text: The Jade plant (Crassula ovata) stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water the Jade plant deeply, then let the top two-thirds of the soil dry before watering again. In spring and summer the Jade plant may need water roughly every two to three weeks, while in winter it may need water only once a month.
cited_quotes: The Jade plant (Crassula ovata) stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water the Jade plant deeply, then let the top two-thirds of the soil dry before watering again. In spring and summer the Jade plant may need water roughly every two to three weeks, while in winter it may need water only once a month. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure with the Jade plant, so err toward keeping it dry. Always empty the saucer so the Jade plant never sits in standing water.

Yellowing fronds across the Boston fern often point to overwatering or poor drainage at the roots. If the Boston fern sheds many leaflets indoors, the most common cause is dry air combined with inconsistent watering.

items.question: How often should I water a Phalaenopsis orchid?
items.answer_text: Water the Orchid (Phalaenopsis) about once every seven to ten days, allowing the potting medium to dry slightly between waterings. Pour room-temperature water over the bark until it drains freely, and never let the Orchid sit in standing water inside a cabinet or saucer. The Orchid needs less water in winter, when watering every ten to fourteen days is usually enough.
cited_quotes: Water the Orchid (Phalaenopsis) about once every seven to ten days, allowing the potting medium to dry slightly between waterings. Pour room-temperature water over the bark until it drains freely, and never let the Orchid sit in standing water inside a cabinet or saucer. The Orchid needs less water in winter, when watering every ten to fourteen days is usually enough. Roots that turn silvery-grey signal that the Orchid is ready for its next drink, while plump green roots mean it has enough moisture. Overwatering is the most common cause of root rot in the Orchid, so err on the drier side.

The most common problem with the Orchid (Phalaenopsis) is root rot from soggy bark, shown by mushy brown roots and wilting leaves. Wrinkled, leathery leaves on the Orchid usually mean underwatering or dehydrated roots rather than too much water. Bud blast, where flower buds yellow and drop before opening, happens when the Orchid faces drafts, sudden temperature swings, or dry air. Sticky residue or small white cottony spots can indicate mealybugs or scale on the Orchid, which you can wipe off with a cotton swab dipped in diluted alcohol. If the Orchid stops blooming, a drop in night temperature of about ten degrees Fahrenheit for a few weeks often triggers a new flower spike.

The cited reference does not list Orchid (Phalaenopsis) as toxic to cats or dogs. The cited reference does not list Orchid as toxic to horses. If a child or pet ingests part of the Orchid and you are concerned, call your local poison-control or veterinary line for guidance. This entry reports only what the cited reference states about the Orchid and does not certify any outcome.

Place the Orchid (Phalaenopsis) in bright, indirect light, such as near an east-facing window where morning sun is gentle. The Orchid will scorch under direct midday sun, so filter strong light through a sheer curtain. Leaves that are a healthy grassy green indicate the Orchid is getting the right amount of light. Dark green, floppy leaves mean the Orchid needs more light, while yellow or reddish leaves suggest too much. A spot with twelve to fourteen hours of daylight encourages the Orchid to rebloom.

Pot the Orchid (Phalaenopsis) in a coarse, free-draining medium such as graded fir bark rather than ordinary houseplant soil. Repot the Orchid every one to two years, ideally just after flowering finishes, to refresh the bark before it breaks down and suffocates the roots. Choose a clear or slotted pot so you can see the Orchid's roots and check moisture at a glance. When repotting, trim away any soft, brown, or hollow roots and keep the firm pale ones. A pot only slightly larger than the old one keeps the Orchid from staying too wet.

items.question: When does a Monstera deliciosa need repotting?
items.answer_text: Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. The Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) grows best in bright, indirect light for roughly 6 to 8 hours a day. The cited reference lists Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, intense burning of the mouth and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing.
cited_quotes: Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. Brown, crispy leaf edges on a Monstera usually indicate low humidity or underwatering, and raising humidity to around 60 percent can help. Few or no leaf splits on a younger Monstera are normal, and fenestration typically increases as the plant matures and receives brighter light. Pests such as spider mites and mealybugs sometimes appear on a Monstera, and wiping the leaves and treating with insecticidal soap usually controls them.

The Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) grows best in bright, indirect light for roughly 6 to 8 hours a day. Direct midday sun can scorch the leaves of a Monstera, leaving pale or brown patches, so filter strong light through a sheer curtain. A Monstera kept in deep shade tends to produce smaller leaves with fewer of the characteristic splits and holes. Rotating the Monstera a quarter turn each week helps it grow evenly toward the light source.

The cited reference lists Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, intense burning of the mouth and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. These effects in the Monstera are caused by insoluble calcium oxalate crystals present throughout the plant's leaves and stems. If a cat or dog chews any part of a Monstera, contact a veterinarian or an animal poison-control line promptly. Keep the Monstera out of reach of pets and children to reduce the chance of accidental ingestion.

items.question: Should I water my Pothos less during the winter months?
items.answer_text: In winter, Pothos needs water less often, roughly every fourteen to twenty-one days, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Water Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) when the top inch of soil has dried out, which is usually every seven to ten days in spring and summer. Pothos prefers to be watered thoroughly until liquid drains from the bottom, and then it should not sit in standing water.
cited_quotes: Water Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) when the top inch of soil has dried out, which is usually every seven to ten days in spring and summer. In winter, Pothos needs water less often, roughly every fourteen to twenty-one days, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Pothos prefers to be watered thoroughly until liquid drains from the bottom, and then it should not sit in standing water. Drooping, soft leaves on a Pothos often signal overwatering, while crispy edges suggest the plant has stayed dry too long. A Pothos tolerates occasional missed waterings better than constantly soggy soil.

Yellowing leaves on a Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) are most commonly caused by overwatering or poor drainage. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a Pothos usually indicate underwatering, low humidity, or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Pothos can attract pests such as spider mites, mealybugs, and scale, which appear as fine webbing, white cottony spots, or small bumps on stems. Leggy, sparse growth on a Pothos points to insufficient light, and moving it to a brighter spot encourages fuller foliage. Wiping the leaves of a Pothos occasionally removes dust and helps the plant absorb more light.

Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) thrives in a loose, well-draining potting mix and dislikes dense soil that holds water around the roots. A blend of standard potting soil with added perlite or orchid bark gives Pothos the aeration it prefers. Repot a Pothos every one to two years, or when roots begin circling the pot or pushing through the drainage holes. When repotting Pothos, choose a container only one to two inches wider than the current one to avoid oversized pots that stay wet. A pot with drainage holes is important for Pothos because trapped moisture leads to root rot.

Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) grows best in bright, indirect light and keeps its variegation strongest under those conditions. A Pothos will survive in low light, but its leaves turn more solidly green and the stems grow leggy with wider gaps between leaves. Direct midday sun can scorch a Pothos, leaving pale or bleached patches on the foliage. If a Pothos loses its yellow or white markings, moving it closer to a bright window usually restores the pattern over several weeks. Pothos does well a few feet from an east- or north-facing window.

El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar un Potho y dejar manchas pálidas o decoloradas en el follaje. Si un Potho pierde sus marcas amarillas o blancas, acercarlo a una ventana luminosa suele restaurar el patrón a lo largo de varias semanas. El Potho se desarrolla bien a un par de pies de una ventana orientada al este o al norte.

El Potho (Epipremnum aureum) prospera en un sustrato suelto y con buen drenaje, y no tolera la tierra densa que retiene agua alrededor de las raíces. Una mezcla de tierra para macetas estándar con perlita o corteza de orquídea añadida le da al Potho la aireación que prefiere. Trasplanta un Potho cada uno o dos años, o cuando las raíces empiecen a enrollarse en la maceta o a salir por los orificios de drenaje. Al trasplantar el Potho, elige un recipiente solo una o dos pulgadas más ancho que el actual para evitar macetas demasiado grandes que permanecen húmedas. Una maceta con orificios de drenaje es importante para el Potho porque la humedad atrapada provoca pudrición de las raíces.

items.question: How much light does a fiddle-leaf fig need?
items.answer_text: The Fiddle-leaf fig prefers bright, indirect light and does best near an east- or south-facing window with a sheer curtain. In low light the Fiddle-leaf fig grows slowly, drops lower leaves, and may lean toward the brightest part of the room. Pale or yellowing lower leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig can point to too little light or a nutrient shortage during active growth.
cited_quotes: The Fiddle-leaf fig prefers bright, indirect light and does best near an east- or south-facing window with a sheer curtain. A few hours of gentle morning sun suit the Fiddle-leaf fig, but harsh midday sun through glass can scorch its large leaves. In low light the Fiddle-leaf fig grows slowly, drops lower leaves, and may lean toward the brightest part of the room. Rotate the Fiddle-leaf fig a quarter turn every week or two so the plant grows evenly on all sides. Keep the Fiddle-leaf fig away from cold drafts and heating vents, which stress the foliage.

Brown spots on a Fiddle-leaf fig often signal overwatering or root rot, especially when the spots start at the leaf edges and the soil stays wet. Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. Pale or yellowing lower leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig can point to too little light or a nutrient shortage during active growth. Wipe the broad leaves of the Fiddle-leaf fig with a damp cloth now and then to clear dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and scale. Steady light, steady watering, and stable temperature prevent most Fiddle-leaf fig problems.

Plant your Fiddle-leaf fig in a well-draining, peat-free potting mix amended with bark or perlite for airflow around the roots. Choose a pot for the Fiddle-leaf fig that has drainage holes, since standing water quickly damages the roots. Repot the Fiddle-leaf fig every 1 to 2 years in spring, moving up just one pot size at a time. When the Fiddle-leaf fig has outgrown the largest practical pot, refresh the top 5 centimeters of soil each spring instead. Firm the mix gently around the base of the Fiddle-leaf fig and water it in after repotting.

The cited reference lists Fiddle-leaf fig (Ficus lyrata) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. The sap of the Fiddle-leaf fig contains irritant compounds that can also cause skin and mouth discomfort on contact. Place the Fiddle-leaf fig out of reach of pets and children, and wash your hands after pruning. If a pet or child has chewed or swallowed part of the Fiddle-leaf fig, contact a veterinarian or a poison-control line right away. This page reports what the source documents and does not certify any outcome for an individual animal.

Water your Fiddle-leaf fig when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in the growing season. Always water the Fiddle-leaf fig thoroughly until liquid drains from the pot, then discard whatever collects in the saucer. Reduce watering for the Fiddle-leaf fig in winter, when the plant uses less moisture and the soil stays damp longer. Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves. Let the moisture level guide your schedule rather than watering on a fixed calendar day.

items.question: How often should I water my snake plant?
items.answer_text: Water snake plant only when the top two inches of soil have dried completely, which is often every two to three weeks in summer. In winter, snake plant needs water much less often, roughly once every four to six weeks. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a snake plant often follow underwatering or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water.
cited_quotes: Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) stores water in its thick upright leaves and tolerates infrequent watering far better than overwatering. Water snake plant only when the top two inches of soil have dried completely, which is often every two to three weeks in summer. In winter, snake plant needs water much less often, roughly once every four to six weeks. Always empty the saucer after watering snake plant, because standing water rots its rhizomes. If the leaves of a snake plant turn soft, mushy, or yellow at the base, the most common cause is too much water.

The most frequent problem with snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) is root rot caused by overwatering, which shows as soft, yellowing, or collapsing leaves. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a snake plant often follow underwatering or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Wrinkled or curling leaves signal that the snake plant is too dry and needs a thorough watering. Cold drafts below 50 degrees Fahrenheit can leave pale scarred patches on snake plant leaves. If a snake plant is not growing, move it to brighter indirect light and resume regular feeding during the growing season.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand. Plant snake plant in a pot with drainage holes, because the rhizomes are prone to rot in waterlogged soil. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years. Repot snake plant in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. Terracotta pots suit snake plant well because the porous clay wicks away excess moisture.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) adapts to a wide range of light, from bright indirect sun to fairly dim corners. The strongest growth and the boldest leaf banding on a snake plant appear in bright, indirect light. A snake plant kept in deep shade survives but grows slowly and produces thinner leaves. Protect snake plant from prolonged direct midday sun through glass, which can scorch and bleach the leaves. Rotating the snake plant a quarter turn every few weeks keeps its upright leaves growing evenly.

The cited reference lists snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, and nausea. The compounds responsible in snake plant are saponins, which irritate the mouth and digestive tract of pets. Keep snake plant out of reach of cats and dogs, and place it where a curious pet cannot chew the leaves. If a cat or dog has eaten any part of a snake plant, contact a veterinarian or an animal poison-control line. The cited reference describes the snake plant reaction as generally mild to moderate, but a professional should still evaluate the animal.

La lengua de suegra (Dracaena trifasciata) se adapta a una amplia gama de luz, desde el sol indirecto brillante hasta rincones bastante tenues. El crecimiento más vigoroso y las bandas más marcadas en las hojas de una lengua de suegra aparecen con luz brillante e indirecta. Una lengua de suegra en sombra profunda sobrevive, pero crece despacio y produce hojas más delgadas. Protege la lengua de suegra del sol directo y prolongado del mediodía a través del vidrio, que puede quemar y decolorar las hojas. Girar la lengua de suegra un cuarto de vuelta cada pocas semanas mantiene sus hojas erguidas creciendo de forma pareja.

items.question: ¿Qué tipo de luz necesita mi Monstera deliciosa?
items.answer_text: La Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta durante unas 6 a 8 horas al día. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar las hojas de una Monstera y dejar manchas pálidas o marrones, así que filtra la luz intensa con una cortina fina. Girar la Monstera un cuarto de vuelta cada semana le ayuda a crecer de forma uniforme hacia la fuente de luz.

Una Monstera mantenida en sombra profunda tiende a producir hojas más pequeñas y con menos de los característicos cortes y agujeros. Riega la Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) cuando los 2 a 3 centímetros superiores del sustrato se hayan secado, lo que suele ocurrir aproximadamente una vez cada 7 a 10 días en crecimiento activo. items.question: ¿Con qué frecuencia debo regar mi lirio de paz?

El Lirio de la paz prefiere luz brillante e indirecta y tolera la luz media o baja mejor que la mayoría de las plantas de interior con flor. Mantén el Lirio de la paz lejos del sol directo del mediodía, porque los rayos directos y calientes pueden quemar sus hojas y dejar manchas marrones. Un lugar a un par de metros de una ventana orientada al este o al norte le sienta bien al Lirio de la paz. Con muy poca luz el Lirio de la paz sobrevivirá, pero puede dejar de producir sus espatas blancas. Si las hojas del Lirio de la paz se ven pálidas o alargadas, trasládalo a un sitio más luminoso con luz filtrada.

Las puntas marrones en las hojas del Lirio de la paz suelen indicar poca humedad, acumulación de minerales del agua del grifo o exceso de fertilizante. Las hojas amarillas en el Lirio de la paz normalmente apuntan a un exceso de riego o a raíces que han estado demasiado tiempo en agua. Si el Lirio de la paz se inclina de forma drástica, revisa primero la tierra, ya que tanto la falta de riego como el exceso severo pueden provocar el marchitamiento. Pocas flores o ninguna en el Lirio de la paz suele significar que la luz es demasiado escasa o que la planta es demasiado joven para florecer.

Planta el Lirio de la paz en un sustrato suelto y con buen drenaje, rico en materia orgánica, como una mezcla a base de turba enmendada con perlita. Elige una maceta con orificios de drenaje, porque el Lirio de la paz no tolera la tierra encharcada. Trasplanta el Lirio de la paz cada uno o dos años en primavera, pasándolo a un recipiente solo una talla más grande. El Lirio de la paz florece de forma más fiable cuando está ligeramente apretado en su maceta, así que evita usar un recipiente demasiado grande. Renueva la capa superior de tierra del Lirio de la paz cada año si no hace falta un trasplante completo.

La referencia citada indica que el Lirio de la paz (Spathiphyllum) es tóxico para gatos y perros; la ingestión puede causar irritación bucal, ardor intenso en la boca y los labios, salivación, vómitos y dificultad para tragar. Estos efectos provienen de los cristales insolubles de oxalato de calcio que contienen las hojas y los tallos del Lirio de la paz. Si un gato o un perro mastica o traga cualquier parte del Lirio de la paz, comunícate de inmediato con un veterinario o con una línea de control de intoxicaciones para mascotas. Mantén el Lirio de la paz fuera del alcance de mascotas y niños, y ten en cuenta que la savia también puede irritar la piel humana.
El Lirio de la paz es distinto de los lirios verdaderos del género Lilium, pero igualmente debe tratarse como peligroso para los animales.

Soft, mushy, or translucent leaves on an Aloe vera usually signal overwatering and the onset of root rot. Thin, curling leaves instead point to underwatering, so check whether the Aloe vera has gone too long without a drink. Brown, crispy leaf tips on Aloe vera can follow sudden exposure to intense direct sun before the plant has acclimated. A pale, stretched, and floppy Aloe vera is reaching for more light and should be moved gradually to a brighter location. If the base of the Aloe vera turns dark and soft, remove the plant, cut away rotted tissue, and repot it in fresh dry succulent mix.

Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) is a succulent that stores water in its leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water Aloe vera deeply but infrequently, allowing the top two inches of soil to become completely dry first. In spring and summer this usually means watering Aloe vera about every two to three weeks, while in winter the interval often stretches to once a month or less. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure with Aloe vera, so when in doubt, wait a few more days before watering. Always discard any water that collects in the saucer so that the roots of your Aloe vera never sit in moisture.

Aloe vera grows best in bright light and tolerates several hours of direct sun once acclimated. Place Aloe vera near a south- or west-facing window where it receives at least six hours of strong light each day. A plant kept in low light will stretch and grow pale, so move a leggy Aloe vera gradually toward a brighter spot to avoid leaf scorch. If you move Aloe vera outdoors for summer, increase sun exposure slowly over one to two weeks. Leaves that turn reddish-brown often indicate that the Aloe vera is receiving more intense sun than it has adjusted to.

El Aloe vera necesita una mezcla de drenaje rápido, así que usa un sustrato para cactus o suculentas enriquecido con perlita adicional o arena gruesa. Planta el Aloe vera en un recipiente con orificios de drenaje, ya que el agua estancada en las raíces conduce rápidamente a la pudrición. Trasplanta el Aloe vera cada dos o tres años, o antes cuando los hijuelos llenen la maceta o las raíces asomen por los orificios de drenaje. Elige una maceta solo una talla más grande, porque un recipiente demasiado grande retiene exceso de humedad alrededor de las raíces del Aloe vera. Después del trasplante, espera alrededor de una semana antes de regar el Aloe vera para que las raíces removidas puedan cicatrizar.

The ZZ plant grows well in low to bright indirect light, which makes the ZZ plant a forgiving choice for dim rooms and offices. Place the ZZ plant near an east- or north-facing window for steady, gentle light. Direct midday sun can scorch the glossy leaves, so keep the ZZ plant out of harsh afternoon rays. The ZZ plant will grow more slowly in very low light but will still survive for months. Rotate the ZZ plant every few weeks so the ZZ plant grows evenly toward the light.

Las hojas amarillentas en una planta ZZ suelen indicar exceso de riego y las primeras etapas de la pudrición de los rizomas. Si la planta ZZ desarrolla tallos blandos o mal olor en la base, reduzca el riego de inmediato y revise los rizomas en busca de pudrición. Las puntas marrones de las hojas en una planta ZZ pueden deberse a aire muy seco o a una acumulación de sales de fertilizante en el sustrato. Pocas plagas molestan a la planta ZZ, aunque pueden aparecer ácaros o cochinillas si la planta ZZ está estresada. Limpie de vez en cuando las hojas de la planta ZZ para quitar el polvo y mantener el follaje brillante.

La planta ZZ almacena agua en sus gruesos rizomas, por lo que la planta ZZ tolera el riego poco frecuente mucho mejor que la mayoría de las plantas de interior. Riegue la planta ZZ solo cuando las 2 pulgadas superiores del sustrato se hayan secado por completo, lo que suele significar cada dos o tres semanas. En invierno la planta ZZ necesita aún menos, y regar una vez al mes suele ser suficiente para la planta ZZ. El exceso de riego es la forma más común de dañar una planta ZZ, porque el sustrato encharcado pudre los rizomas. En caso de duda, deje seca la planta ZZ en lugar de tomar la regadera.

La planta ZZ crece bien con luz indirecta de baja a brillante intensidad, lo que hace de la planta ZZ una opción tolerante para habitaciones poco iluminadas y oficinas. Coloque la planta ZZ cerca de una ventana orientada al este o al norte para recibir luz suave y constante. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar las hojas brillantes, así que mantenga la planta ZZ alejada de los rayos fuertes de la tarde. La planta ZZ crecerá más despacio con muy poca luz, pero aun así sobrevivirá durante meses. Gire la planta ZZ cada pocas semanas para que la planta ZZ crezca de forma pareja hacia la luz.

The ZZ plant stores water in its thick rhizomes, so the ZZ plant tolerates infrequent watering far better than most houseplants. Water the ZZ plant only when the top 2 inches of soil have dried out completely, which often means every two to three weeks. items.question: How often should I water my Monstera deliciosa?
items.answer_text: Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering.
cited_quotes: Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. Let the Monstera drain fully after watering and never leave the pot sitting in standing water. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Drooping or yellowing lower leaves on a Monstera frequently signal overwatering rather than thirst, so check the soil before adding more water.

Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. Brown, crispy leaf edges on a Monstera usually indicate low humidity or underwatering, and raising humidity to around 60 percent can help. Riega la Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) cuando los 2 a 3 centímetros superiores del sustrato se hayan secado, lo que suele ocurrir aproximadamente una vez cada 7 a 10 días en crecimiento activo. Deja que la Monstera drene por completo después de regar y nunca dejes la maceta sobre agua estancada. En invierno la Monstera necesita riegos menos frecuentes, a menudo solo una vez cada 2 a 3 semanas, porque el crecimiento se ralentiza y el sustrato permanece húmedo más tiempo. Las hojas inferiores caídas o amarillentas en una Monstera suelen indicar exceso de riego en lugar de sed, así que revisa el sustrato antes de añadir más agua.

Plant the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) in a loose, well-draining potting mix amended with bark, perlite, or coir to keep roots aerated. Choose a pot for the Monstera that has drainage holes and is only 2 to 5 centimeters wider than the current root ball. Repot the Monstera every 1 to 2 years in spring when roots begin circling the pot or emerging from the drainage holes. A mature Monstera benefits from a moss pole or stake, because its aerial roots will climb and support larger, more fenestrated leaves.

Planta la Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) en una mezcla suelta y de buen drenaje, enriquecida con corteza, perlita o fibra de coco para mantener las raíces aireadas. Elige para la Monstera una maceta con orificios de drenaje y solo 2 a 5 centímetros más ancha que el cepellón actual. Trasplanta la Monstera cada 1 a 2 años en primavera, cuando las raíces empiecen a dar vueltas en la maceta o a salir por los orificios de drenaje. items.question: What light conditions does a Pothos need to thrive indoors?
items.answer_text: Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) grows best in bright, indirect light and keeps its variegation strongest under those conditions. A Pothos will survive in low light, but its leaves turn more solidly green and the stems grow leggy with wider gaps between leaves. Leggy, sparse growth on a Pothos points to insufficient light, and moving it to a brighter spot encourages fuller foliage.
cited_quotes: Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) grows best in bright, indirect light and keeps its variegation strongest under those conditions. A Pothos will survive in low light, but its leaves turn more solidly green and the stems grow leggy with wider gaps between leaves. Direct midday sun can scorch a Pothos, leaving pale or bleached patches on the foliage. If a Pothos loses its yellow or white markings, moving it closer to a bright window usually restores the pattern over several weeks. Pothos does well a few feet from an east- or north-facing window.

Yellowing leaves on a Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) are most commonly caused by overwatering or poor drainage. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a Pothos usually indicate underwatering, low humidity, or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Pothos can attract pests such as spider mites, mealybugs, and scale, which appear as fine webbing, white cottony spots, or small bumps on stems. Leggy, sparse growth on a Pothos points to insufficient light, and moving it to a brighter spot encourages fuller foliage. Wiping the leaves of a Pothos occasionally removes dust and helps the plant absorb more light.

El Potho (Epipremnum aureum) crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta y mantiene su variegación más intensa en esas condiciones. Un Potho sobrevivirá con poca luz, pero sus hojas se vuelven de un verde más uniforme y los tallos se alargan con mayores espacios entre las hojas. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar un Potho y dejar manchas pálidas o decoloradas en el follaje. Si un Potho pierde sus marcas amarillas o blancas, acercarlo a una ventana luminosa suele restaurar el patrón a lo largo de varias semanas. El Potho se desarrolla bien a un par de pies de una ventana orientada al este o al norte.

Water Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) when the top inch of soil has dried out, which is usually every seven to ten days in spring and summer. In winter, Pothos needs water less often, roughly every fourteen to twenty-one days, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Pothos prefers to be watered thoroughly until liquid drains from the bottom, and then it should not sit in standing water. Drooping, soft leaves on a Pothos often signal overwatering, while crispy edges suggest the plant has stayed dry too long. A Pothos tolerates occasional missed waterings better than constantly soggy soil.

Las hojas amarillentas en un Potho (Epipremnum aureum) se deben con mayor frecuencia al exceso de riego o al drenaje deficiente. Las puntas de las hojas marrones y secas en un Potho suelen indicar falta de riego, baja humedad o acumulación de sales minerales del agua del grifo. El Potho puede atraer plagas como ácaros, cochinillas algodonosas y cochinillas con caparazón, que aparecen como telarañas finas, manchas blancas algodonosas o pequeños bultos en los tallos. El crecimiento alargado y escaso en un Potho indica luz insuficiente, y trasladarlo a un lugar más brillante favorece un follaje más tupido. Limpiar las hojas del Potho de vez en cuando elimina el polvo y ayuda a la planta a absorber más luz.

Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) thrives in a loose, well-draining potting mix and dislikes dense soil that holds water around the roots. A blend of standard potting soil with added perlite or orchid bark gives Pothos the aeration it prefers. Repot a Pothos every one to two years, or when roots begin circling the pot or pushing through the drainage holes. When repotting Pothos, choose a container only one to two inches wider than the current one to avoid oversized pots that stay wet. A pot with drainage holes is important for Pothos because trapped moisture leads to root rot.

Un Potho sobrevivirá con poca luz, pero sus hojas se vuelven de un verde más uniforme y los tallos se alargan con mayores espacios entre las hojas. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar un Potho y dejar manchas pálidas o decoloradas en el follaje. Si un Potho pierde sus marcas amarillas o blancas, acercarlo a una ventana luminosa suele restaurar el patrón a lo largo de varias semanas. El Potho se desarrolla bien a un par de pies de una ventana orientada al este o al norte.

Las hojas amarillentas en un Potho (Epipremnum aureum) se deben con mayor frecuencia al exceso de riego o al drenaje deficiente. Las puntas de las hojas marrones y secas en un Potho suelen indicar falta de riego, baja humedad o acumulación de sales minerales del agua del grifo. El Potho puede atraer plagas como ácaros, cochinillas algodonosas y cochinillas con caparazón, que aparecen como telarañas finas, manchas blancas algodonosas o pequeños bultos en los tallos. El crecimiento alargado y escaso en un Potho indica luz insuficiente, y trasladarlo a un lugar más brillante favorece un follaje más tupido. Limpiar las hojas del Potho de vez en cuando elimina el polvo y ayuda a la planta a absorber más luz.

Riega el Potho (Epipremnum aureum) cuando la primera pulgada de tierra se haya secado, lo que suele ocurrir cada siete a diez días en primavera y verano. En invierno, el Potho necesita agua con menos frecuencia, aproximadamente cada catorce a veintiún días, porque el crecimiento se ralentiza y la tierra permanece húmeda más tiempo. El Potho prefiere regarse a fondo hasta que el líquido drene por la base, y luego no debe quedar en agua estancada. Las hojas caídas y blandas en un Potho suelen indicar exceso de riego, mientras que los bordes secos sugieren que la planta estuvo demasiado tiempo sin agua. Un Potho tolera mejor un riego olvidado de vez en cuando que la tierra constantemente empapada.

The cited reference lists Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, intense burning of the mouth and tongue, excessive drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. These effects in Pothos are attributed to insoluble calcium oxalate crystals released when an animal chews the leaves or stems. If a cat or dog is suspected of chewing or swallowing Pothos, contact a veterinarian or a poison-control hotline promptly. Keeping Pothos out of reach of pets is the surest way to prevent accidental ingestion.

El Potho (Epipremnum aureum) prospera en un sustrato suelto y con buen drenaje, y no tolera la tierra densa que retiene agua alrededor de las raíces. Una mezcla de tierra para macetas estándar con perlita o corteza de orquídea añadida le da al Potho la aireación que prefiere. Trasplanta un Potho cada uno o dos años, o cuando las raíces empiecen a enrollarse en la maceta o a salir por los orificios de drenaje. Al trasplantar el Potho, elige un recipiente solo una o dos pulgadas más ancho que el actual para evitar macetas demasiado grandes que permanecen húmedas. Una maceta con orificios de drenaje es importante para el Potho porque la humedad atrapada provoca pudrición de las raíces.

Water Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) when the top inch of soil has dried out, which is usually every seven to ten days in spring and summer. In winter, Pothos needs water less often, roughly every fourteen to twenty-one days, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Pothos prefers to be watered thoroughly until liquid drains from the bottom, and then it should not sit in standing water. Drooping, soft leaves on a Pothos often signal overwatering, while crispy edges suggest the plant has stayed dry too long. A Pothos tolerates occasional missed waterings better than constantly soggy soil.

items.question: What are the signs that my snake plant is being overwatered?
items.answer_text: The most frequent problem with snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) is root rot caused by overwatering, which shows as soft, yellowing, or collapsing leaves. Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) stores water in its thick upright leaves and tolerates infrequent watering far better than overwatering. Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand.
cited_quotes: The most frequent problem with snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) is root rot caused by overwatering, which shows as soft, yellowing, or collapsing leaves. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a snake plant often follow underwatering or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Wrinkled or curling leaves signal that the snake plant is too dry and needs a thorough watering. Cold drafts below 50 degrees Fahrenheit can leave pale scarred patches on snake plant leaves. If a snake plant is not growing, move it to brighter indirect light and resume regular feeding during the growing season.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) stores water in its thick upright leaves and tolerates infrequent watering far better than overwatering. Water snake plant only when the top two inches of soil have dried completely, which is often every two to three weeks in summer. In winter, snake plant needs water much less often, roughly once every four to six weeks. Always empty the saucer after watering snake plant, because standing water rots its rhizomes. If the leaves of a snake plant turn soft, mushy, or yellow at the base, the most common cause is too much water.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand. Plant snake plant in a pot with drainage holes, because the rhizomes are prone to rot in waterlogged soil. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years. Repot snake plant in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. Terracotta pots suit snake plant well because the porous clay wicks away excess moisture.

items.question: Why are the leaves on my peace lily drooping?
items.answer_text: Yellowing leaves on the Peace lily usually point to overwatering or roots that have been sitting in water too long. If the Peace lily droops dramatically, check the soil first, as both underwatering and severe overwatering can cause wilting. Wipe the broad leaves of the Peace lily occasionally to remove dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and mealybugs.
cited_quotes: Brown leaf tips on a Peace lily often signal low humidity, mineral buildup from tap water, or over-fertilizing. Yellowing leaves on the Peace lily usually point to overwatering or roots that have been sitting in water too long. If the Peace lily droops dramatically, check the soil first, as both underwatering and severe overwatering can cause wilting. Few or no flowers on the Peace lily commonly mean the light is too low or the plant is too young to bloom. Wipe the broad leaves of the Peace lily occasionally to remove dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and mealybugs.
