The cited reference lists Peace lily (Spathiphyllum) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, intense burning of the mouth and lips, drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. These effects come from insoluble calcium oxalate crystals contained in the Peace lily's leaves and stems. If a cat or dog chews or swallows any part of the Peace lily, contact a veterinarian or a pet poison-control line promptly. Keep the Peace lily out of reach of pets and children, and note that the sap can also irritate human skin. The Peace lily is distinct from true lilies of the genus Lilium, but it should still be treated as hazardous to animals.

The Peace lily prefers bright, indirect light and tolerates medium to low light better than most flowering houseplants. Keep the Peace lily out of direct midday sun, because hot direct rays can scorch its leaves and leave brown patches. A spot a few feet back from an east- or north-facing window suits the Peace lily well. In very low light the Peace lily will survive but it may stop producing its white flowering spathes. If the Peace lily's leaves look pale or leggy, move it to a brighter location with filtered light.

Plant the Peace lily in a loose, well-draining potting mix rich in organic matter, such as a peat-based mix amended with perlite. Choose a pot with drainage holes, because the Peace lily will not tolerate waterlogged soil. Repot the Peace lily every one to two years in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. The Peace lily actually flowers more reliably when it is slightly root-bound, so avoid overpotting. Refresh the top layer of soil for the Peace lily each year if a full repot is not needed.

Water the Peace lily when the top inch of soil feels dry to the touch, which is roughly once every five to seven days in warm months. The Peace lily wilts visibly when it is thirsty, and it usually recovers within a few hours of a thorough watering. Reduce watering for the Peace lily in winter to about once every ten to fourteen days, because the plant grows slowly and the soil stays wet longer. Always let excess water drain away, since the Peace lily is prone to root rot if its roots sit in standing water. Use room-temperature water and empty the saucer after watering the Peace lily.

items.question: ¿Por qué se caen las hojas de mi lirio de la paz?
items.answer_text: Mantén el Lirio de la paz lejos del sol directo del mediodía, porque los rayos directos y calientes pueden quemar sus hojas y dejar manchas marrones. Si las hojas del Lirio de la paz se ven pálidas o alargadas, trasládalo a un sitio más luminoso con luz filtrada. Las puntas marrones en las hojas del Lirio de la paz suelen indicar poca humedad, acumulación de minerales del agua del grifo o exceso de fertilizante.
cited_quotes: El Lirio de la paz prefiere luz brillante e indirecta y tolera la luz media o baja mejor que la mayoría de las plantas de interior con flor. Mantén el Lirio de la paz lejos del sol directo del mediodía, porque los rayos directos y calientes pueden quemar sus hojas y dejar manchas marrones. Un lugar a un par de metros de una ventana orientada al este o al norte le sienta bien al Lirio de la paz. Con muy poca luz el Lirio de la paz sobrevivirá, pero puede dejar de producir sus espatas blancas. Si las hojas del Lirio de la paz se ven pálidas o alargadas, trasládalo a un sitio más luminoso con luz filtrada.

Las puntas marrones en las hojas del Lirio de la paz suelen indicar poca humedad, acumulación de minerales del agua del grifo o exceso de fertilizante. Las hojas amarillas en el Lirio de la paz normalmente apuntan a un exceso de riego o a raíces que han estado demasiado tiempo en agua. Si el Lirio de la paz se inclina de forma drástica, revisa primero la tierra, ya que tanto la falta de riego como el exceso severo pueden provocar el marchitamiento. Pocas flores o ninguna en el Lirio de la paz suele significar que la luz es demasiado escasa o que la planta es demasiado joven para florecer.

Plant Philodendron in a loose, well-draining mix, such as potting soil amended with bark, perlite, or coir. Choose a pot for your Philodendron with drainage holes so excess water can escape freely. Repot a Philodendron every one to two years, or when roots circle the bottom or grow out of the drainage holes. Move Philodendron into a container only one to two inches wider, because an oversized pot holds excess moisture around the roots. The best time to repot a Philodendron is in spring or early summer during active growth.

Yellowing leaves on a Philodendron most often point to overwatering, while crispy brown leaf edges suggest the air is too dry or the soil stayed dry too long. Brown spots on Philodendron foliage can follow direct sun exposure or cold drafts from a window or door. Leggy, sparse growth tells you a Philodendron needs brighter, indirect light. Inspect a Philodendron regularly for spider mites, mealybugs, and aphids, and wipe the leaves or treat with insecticidal soap if pests appear. Wiping the leaves of a Philodendron with a damp cloth removes dust and helps the plant breathe and photosynthesize.

Water Philodendron when the top one to two inches of soil have dried out, which is often about once a week in spring and summer. Allow Philodendron to dry more between waterings in fall and winter, watering roughly every ten to fourteen days as growth slows. Philodendron prefers soil that is evenly moist but never waterlogged, so pour off any water left in the saucer after about fifteen minutes. Drooping or yellowing lower leaves on a Philodendron often signal overwatering rather than thirst. When in doubt, wait an extra day, because Philodendron tolerates a brief dry spell better than soggy roots.

items.question: What causes brown spots on the leaves of my fiddle-leaf fig?
items.answer_text: Brown spots on a Fiddle-leaf fig often signal overwatering or root rot, especially when the spots start at the leaf edges and the soil stays wet. Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. Pale or yellowing lower leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig can point to too little light or a nutrient shortage during active growth.
cited_quotes: Brown spots on a Fiddle-leaf fig often signal overwatering or root rot, especially when the spots start at the leaf edges and the soil stays wet. Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. Pale or yellowing lower leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig can point to too little light or a nutrient shortage during active growth. Wipe the broad leaves of the Fiddle-leaf fig with a damp cloth now and then to clear dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and scale. Steady light, steady watering, and stable temperature prevent most Fiddle-leaf fig problems.

The Fiddle-leaf fig prefers bright, indirect light and does best near an east- or south-facing window with a sheer curtain. A few hours of gentle morning sun suit the Fiddle-leaf fig, but harsh midday sun through glass can scorch its large leaves. In low light the Fiddle-leaf fig grows slowly, drops lower leaves, and may lean toward the brightest part of the room. Rotate the Fiddle-leaf fig a quarter turn every week or two so the plant grows evenly on all sides. Keep the Fiddle-leaf fig away from cold drafts and heating vents, which stress the foliage.

Plant your Fiddle-leaf fig in a well-draining, peat-free potting mix amended with bark or perlite for airflow around the roots. Choose a pot for the Fiddle-leaf fig that has drainage holes, since standing water quickly damages the roots. Repot the Fiddle-leaf fig every 1 to 2 years in spring, moving up just one pot size at a time. When the Fiddle-leaf fig has outgrown the largest practical pot, refresh the top 5 centimeters of soil each spring instead. Firm the mix gently around the base of the Fiddle-leaf fig and water it in after repotting.

Water your Fiddle-leaf fig when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in the growing season. Always water the Fiddle-leaf fig thoroughly until liquid drains from the pot, then discard whatever collects in the saucer. Reduce watering for the Fiddle-leaf fig in winter, when the plant uses less moisture and the soil stays damp longer. Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves. Let the moisture level guide your schedule rather than watering on a fixed calendar day.

Mantén el Ficus lira lejos de corrientes frías y de salidas de calefacción, que estresan el follaje.

items.question: When should I repot my rubber plant and into what size pot?
items.answer_text: A pot with drainage holes is important for the Rubber plant because the roots will rot in soil that stays saturated. The Rubber plant is typically repotted every two to three years, or when roots begin circling the pot or emerging from the drainage holes. When repotting the Rubber plant, choose a container only one size larger to avoid leaving excess wet soil around the roots.
cited_quotes: The Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) does best in a well-draining potting mix, such as a general houseplant mix amended with perlite or bark. A pot with drainage holes is important for the Rubber plant because the roots will rot in soil that stays saturated. The Rubber plant is typically repotted every two to three years, or when roots begin circling the pot or emerging from the drainage holes. When repotting the Rubber plant, choose a container only one size larger to avoid leaving excess wet soil around the roots. Spring is the preferred time to repot the Rubber plant, as it recovers fastest during active growth.

The Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) grows best in bright, indirect light near an east- or south-facing window. The Rubber plant can adapt to medium light, but its growth slows and the lower leaves may drop in dim conditions. Harsh direct midday sun can scorch the leaves of the Rubber plant, leaving brown or bleached patches. Variegated forms of the Rubber plant need brighter light than the all-green forms to keep their coloring. Rotating the Rubber plant a quarter turn each week helps it grow evenly toward the light.

The Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) prefers to have the top inch or two of soil dry out before the next watering. During the active growing season the Rubber plant is typically watered about once every seven to ten days, depending on light and indoor humidity. In winter the Rubber plant uses far less water, so watering once every two to three weeks is often enough. Overwatering the Rubber plant is a common cause of yellowing lower leaves and root rot, so the pot must drain freely. When watering the Rubber plant, water thoroughly until liquid runs from the drainage holes, then discard any water left in the saucer.

The cited reference lists Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, drooling, vomiting, and skin irritation from the milky sap. The milky latex sap of the Rubber plant can also irritate the skin of people who handle damaged stems or leaves. If a cat or dog is suspected of chewing or swallowing part of a Rubber plant, contact a veterinarian or an animal poison-control line promptly. Keep the Rubber plant out of reach of pets and children, and wash hands after pruning. This reference does not replace professional veterinary or medical advice about a specific Rubber plant exposure.

Yellowing and dropping lower leaves on a Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) most often signal overwatering or poor drainage. Brown, crispy leaf edges on the Rubber plant usually point to underwatering, low humidity, or salt buildup from fertilizer. Sudden leaf drop on the Rubber plant is frequently a response to cold drafts, relocation, or a sharp change in light. Dust accumulating on the broad leaves of the Rubber plant reduces light capture, so the leaves benefit from an occasional gentle wipe with a damp cloth. Common pests on the Rubber plant include scale, mealybugs, and spider mites, which can be managed by wiping the leaves and treating with insecticidal soap.

El exceso de riego del árbol del caucho es una causa común del amarilleo de las hojas inferiores y de la pudrición de raíces, por lo que la maceta debe drenar libremente.

items.question: How should I adjust watering for my aloe vera in winter?
items.answer_text: In spring and summer this usually means watering Aloe vera about every two to three weeks, while in winter the interval often stretches to once a month or less. Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) is a succulent that stores water in its leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water Aloe vera deeply but infrequently, allowing the top two inches of soil to become completely dry first.

Aloe vera grows best in bright light and tolerates several hours of direct sun once acclimated. Place Aloe vera near a south- or west-facing window where it receives at least six hours of strong light each day. A plant kept in low light will stretch and grow pale, so move a leggy Aloe vera gradually toward a brighter spot to avoid leaf scorch. If you move Aloe vera outdoors for summer, increase sun exposure slowly over one to two weeks. Leaves that turn reddish-brown often indicate that the Aloe vera is receiving more intense sun than it has adjusted to.

Soft, mushy, or translucent leaves on an Aloe vera usually signal overwatering and the onset of root rot. Thin, curling leaves instead point to underwatering, so check whether the Aloe vera has gone too long without a drink. Brown, crispy leaf tips on Aloe vera can follow sudden exposure to intense direct sun before the plant has acclimated. A pale, stretched, and floppy Aloe vera is reaching for more light and should be moved gradually to a brighter location. If the base of the Aloe vera turns dark and soft, remove the plant, cut away rotted tissue, and repot it in fresh dry succulent mix.

El Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) es una suculenta que almacena agua en sus hojas y prefiere secarse por completo entre riegos. Riega el Aloe vera de forma profunda pero poco frecuente, dejando que las dos pulgadas superiores del sustrato se sequen completamente primero. En primavera y verano esto suele significar regar el Aloe vera cada dos o tres semanas, mientras que en invierno el intervalo a menudo se alarga a una vez al mes o menos. El exceso de riego es la causa más común de fracaso con el Aloe vera, así que ante la duda, espera unos días más antes de regar.

El Aloe vera necesita una mezcla de drenaje rápido, así que usa un sustrato para cactus o suculentas enriquecido con perlita adicional o arena gruesa. Planta el Aloe vera en un recipiente con orificios de drenaje, ya que el agua estancada en las raíces conduce rápidamente a la pudrición. Trasplanta el Aloe vera cada dos o tres años, o antes cuando los hijuelos llenen la maceta o las raíces asomen por los orificios de drenaje. Elige una maceta solo una talla más grande, porque un recipiente demasiado grande retiene exceso de humedad alrededor de las raíces del Aloe vera. Después del trasplante, espera alrededor de una semana antes de regar el Aloe vera para que las raíces removidas puedan cicatrizar.

items.question: Why are the fronds on my Boston fern turning yellow and crispy?
items.answer_text: Yellowing fronds across the Boston fern often point to overwatering or poor drainage at the roots. Browning frond tips on the Boston fern usually signal low humidity, underwatering, or excess fertilizer salts in the soil. Trimming dead fronds at the base helps the Boston fern channel energy into healthy new growth.
cited_quotes: Browning frond tips on the Boston fern usually signal low humidity, underwatering, or excess fertilizer salts in the soil. Yellowing fronds across the Boston fern often point to overwatering or poor drainage at the roots. If the Boston fern sheds many leaflets indoors, the most common cause is dry air combined with inconsistent watering. Inspect the Boston fern for scale insects and spider mites, which appear when the air is too dry and warm. Trimming dead fronds at the base helps the Boston fern channel energy into healthy new growth.

The Boston fern grows best in bright, indirect light and tolerates moderate shade. Place the Boston fern near an east-facing or north-facing window where it receives filtered daylight rather than direct sun. Harsh midday sun will scorch the fronds of the Boston fern and bleach their green color. If the Boston fern is kept in deep shade, its growth slows and new fronds emerge thin and sparse. A spot that stays between 18 and 24 degrees Celsius suits the Boston fern well throughout the year.

The Boston fern prefers soil that stays evenly and consistently moist but never waterlogged. Water the Boston fern whenever the top half inch of the potting mix begins to feel dry to the touch. In a warm, well-lit room the Boston fern often needs watering two or three times per week, while in winter once every five to seven days is usually enough. Because the Boston fern resents dry air, mist its fronds or set the pot on a humidity tray to keep relative humidity near 50 to 70 percent. Allowing the Boston fern to dry out completely will cause the delicate leaflets to brown and drop.

The cited reference does not list the Boston fern (Nephrolepis exaltata) as toxic to cats or dogs. According to the cited reference, the Boston fern is not associated with poisoning in household pets that nibble its fronds. Even so, any plant material can cause mild stomach upset if a cat or dog eats a large amount, so the Boston fern is best kept out of a pet's regular reach. If a pet shows unusual symptoms after contact with the Boston fern, contact a veterinarian or a poison-control line for guidance. The cited reference addresses only toxicity and does not evaluate choking or other physical hazards.

El helecho de Boston prospera en una mezcla suelta a base de turba o de fibra de coco que drene libremente y a la vez retenga humedad. Elige para el helecho de Boston una maceta con orificios de drenaje, ya que el agua estancada pudre sus raíces finas. Trasplanta el helecho de Boston cada uno o dos años en primavera, pasándolo a una maceta una talla mayor cuando las raíces llenen el recipiente. Al trasplantar el helecho de Boston, puedes dividir una mata grande en dos o tres plantas más pequeñas para propagarlo. Un abonado mensual ligero con fertilizante equilibrado diluido durante la primavera y el verano mantiene frondoso al helecho de Boston.

El helecho de Boston crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta y tolera la sombra moderada. Coloca el helecho de Boston cerca de una ventana orientada al este o al norte, donde reciba luz natural filtrada en lugar de sol directo. El sol fuerte del mediodía quemará las frondas del helecho de Boston y descolorará su tono verde. Si el helecho de Boston se mantiene en sombra profunda, su crecimiento se ralentiza y las frondas nuevas salen finas y escasas. Un lugar que se mantenga entre 18 y 24 grados Celsius le conviene al helecho de Boston durante todo el año.

items.question: ¿Por qué las frondas de mi helecho de Boston se vuelven amarillas y quebradizas?
items.answer_text: Las puntas marrones de las frondas del helecho de Boston suelen indicar baja humedad, riego insuficiente o exceso de sales de fertilizante en el sustrato. Las frondas amarillentas en todo el helecho de Boston a menudo apuntan a un exceso de riego o a un drenaje deficiente en las raíces. Recortar las frondas muertas en la base ayuda al helecho de Boston a dirigir su energía hacia un crecimiento nuevo y sano.

Planta el Lirio de la paz en un sustrato suelto y con buen drenaje, rico en materia orgánica, como una mezcla a base de turba enmendada con perlita. Elige una maceta con orificios de drenaje, porque el Lirio de la paz no tolera la tierra encharcada. Trasplanta el Lirio de la paz cada uno o dos años en primavera, pasándolo a un recipiente solo una talla más grande. El Lirio de la paz florece de forma más fiable cuando está ligeramente apretado en su maceta, así que evita usar un recipiente demasiado grande. Renueva la capa superior de tierra del Lirio de la paz cada año si no hace falta un trasplante completo.

El Lirio de la paz prefiere luz brillante e indirecta y tolera la luz media o baja mejor que la mayoría de las plantas de interior con flor. Mantén el Lirio de la paz lejos del sol directo del mediodía, porque los rayos directos y calientes pueden quemar sus hojas y dejar manchas marrones. Un lugar a un par de metros de una ventana orientada al este o al norte le sienta bien al Lirio de la paz. Con muy poca luz el Lirio de la paz sobrevivirá, pero puede dejar de producir sus espatas blancas. Si las hojas del Lirio de la paz se ven pálidas o alargadas, trasládalo a un sitio más luminoso con luz filtrada.

Las puntas marrones en las hojas del Lirio de la paz suelen indicar poca humedad, acumulación de minerales del agua del grifo o exceso de fertilizante. Las hojas amarillas en el Lirio de la paz normalmente apuntan a un exceso de riego o a raíces que han estado demasiado tiempo en agua. Si el Lirio de la paz se inclina de forma drástica, revisa primero la tierra, ya que tanto la falta de riego como el exceso severo pueden provocar el marchitamiento. Pocas flores o ninguna en el Lirio de la paz suele significar que la luz es demasiado escasa o que la planta es demasiado joven para florecer.
El Lirio de la paz es distinto de los lirios verdaderos del género Lilium, pero igualmente debe tratarse como peligroso para los animales.

Riega el Lirio de la paz cuando los primeros dos o tres centímetros de tierra estén secos al tacto, lo que suele ocurrir cada cinco a siete días en los meses cálidos. El Lirio de la paz se marchita de forma visible cuando tiene sed, y normalmente se recupera en pocas horas tras un riego abundante. Reduce el riego del Lirio de la paz en invierno a una vez cada diez a catorce días, porque la planta crece despacio y la tierra permanece húmeda más tiempo. Deja siempre que el exceso de agua drene, ya que el Lirio de la paz es propenso a la pudrición de raíces si estas quedan en agua estancada.

items.question: How often should I water my Monstera deliciosa in summer, and how do I know when it's ready?
items.answer_text: Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering.
cited_quotes: Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. Let the Monstera drain fully after watering and never leave the pot sitting in standing water. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Drooping or yellowing lower leaves on a Monstera frequently signal overwatering rather than thirst, so check the soil before adding more water.

Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering. Brown, crispy leaf edges on a Monstera usually indicate low humidity or underwatering, and raising humidity to around 60 percent can help. Few or no leaf splits on a younger Monstera are normal, and fenestration typically increases as the plant matures and receives brighter light. Pests such as spider mites and mealybugs sometimes appear on a Monstera, and wiping the leaves and treating with insecticidal soap usually controls them.

items.question: My Pothos vines are getting long and leggy with big gaps between leaves — how should I prune it?
items.answer_text: A Pothos will survive in low light, but its leaves turn more solidly green and the stems grow leggy with wider gaps between leaves. Drooping, soft leaves on a Pothos often signal overwatering, while crispy edges suggest the plant has stayed dry too long.
cited_quotes: Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) grows best in bright, indirect light and keeps its variegation strongest under those conditions. A Pothos will survive in low light, but its leaves turn more solidly green and the stems grow leggy with wider gaps between leaves. Direct midday sun can scorch a Pothos, leaving pale or bleached patches on the foliage. If a Pothos loses its yellow or white markings, moving it closer to a bright window usually restores the pattern over several weeks. Pothos does well a few feet from an east- or north-facing window.

Water Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) when the top inch of soil has dried out, which is usually every seven to ten days in spring and summer. In winter, Pothos needs water less often, roughly every fourteen to twenty-one days, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Pothos prefers to be watered thoroughly until liquid drains from the bottom, and then it should not sit in standing water. Drooping, soft leaves on a Pothos often signal overwatering, while crispy edges suggest the plant has stayed dry too long. A Pothos tolerates occasional missed waterings better than constantly soggy soil.

items.question: What light conditions does a snake plant prefer, and can it tolerate a low-light hallway?
items.answer_text: Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) adapts to a wide range of light, from bright indirect sun to fairly dim corners. The strongest growth and the boldest leaf banding on a snake plant appear in bright, indirect light. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years.
cited_quotes: Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) adapts to a wide range of light, from bright indirect sun to fairly dim corners. The strongest growth and the boldest leaf banding on a snake plant appear in bright, indirect light. A snake plant kept in deep shade survives but grows slowly and produces thinner leaves. Protect snake plant from prolonged direct midday sun through glass, which can scorch and bleach the leaves. Rotating the snake plant a quarter turn every few weeks keeps its upright leaves growing evenly.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand. Plant snake plant in a pot with drainage holes, because the rhizomes are prone to rot in waterlogged soil. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years. Repot snake plant in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. Terracotta pots suit snake plant well because the porous clay wicks away excess moisture.

items.question: The tips of my spider plant's leaves are turning brown — what usually causes that and how do I fix it?
items.answer_text: Brown leaf tips are the most common complaint with the Spider plant and usually trace to fluoride, chlorine, or salt buildup in the soil. The Spider plant is sensitive to fluoride and chlorine, so let tap water sit overnight or use filtered water to prevent brown leaf tips. Brown tips on a Spider plant often signal mineral buildup or inconsistent watering rather than underwatering alone.
cited_quotes: Brown leaf tips are the most common complaint with the Spider plant and usually trace to fluoride, chlorine, or salt buildup in the soil. Flush the Spider plant's soil with filtered water every few months to wash out accumulated minerals. Pale or limp foliage on a Spider plant can indicate too much direct sun or overwatering, so check the light and the moisture before adjusting care. The Spider plant can attract spider mites and aphids in dry indoor air, so inspect the undersides of leaves and wipe them down regularly. A healthy Spider plant produces baby plantlets on long stems, and these can be rooted in water or soil to grow new plants.

Water the Spider plant when the top inch of soil has dried out, which is roughly once every seven to ten days in spring and summer. Reduce watering for the Spider plant in winter to about once every two weeks, since growth slows and the soil stays damp longer. The Spider plant is sensitive to fluoride and chlorine, so let tap water sit overnight or use filtered water to prevent brown leaf tips. Allow excess water to drain fully, because the Spider plant will not tolerate sitting in a saturated saucer. Brown tips on a Spider plant often signal mineral buildup or inconsistent watering rather than underwatering alone.

items.question: ¿Con qué frecuencia debo regar mi orquídea Phalaenopsis y cómo sé que necesita agua?
items.answer_text: La Orquídea necesita menos agua en invierno, cuando regar cada diez a catorce días suele ser suficiente.

La Orquídea necesita menos agua en invierno, cuando regar cada diez a catorce días suele ser suficiente. items.question: ¿Qué tipo de luz necesita un helecho de Boston y puedo ponerlo cerca de una ventana brillante?
items.answer_text: Coloca el helecho de Boston cerca de una ventana orientada al este o al norte, donde reciba luz natural filtrada en lugar de sol directo. El helecho de Boston crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta y tolera la sombra moderada. Como el helecho de Boston no tolera el aire seco, rocía sus frondas o coloca la maceta sobre una bandeja de humedad para mantener la humedad relativa cerca del 50 al 70 por ciento.

items.question: My fiddle-leaf fig is dropping leaves after I moved it across the room — what's likely going on?
items.answer_text: In low light the Fiddle-leaf fig grows slowly, drops lower leaves, and may lean toward the brightest part of the room. Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves.
cited_quotes: The Fiddle-leaf fig prefers bright, indirect light and does best near an east- or south-facing window with a sheer curtain. A few hours of gentle morning sun suit the Fiddle-leaf fig, but harsh midday sun through glass can scorch its large leaves. In low light the Fiddle-leaf fig grows slowly, drops lower leaves, and may lean toward the brightest part of the room. Rotate the Fiddle-leaf fig a quarter turn every week or two so the plant grows evenly on all sides. Keep the Fiddle-leaf fig away from cold drafts and heating vents, which stress the foliage.

Brown spots on a Fiddle-leaf fig often signal overwatering or root rot, especially when the spots start at the leaf edges and the soil stays wet. Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. Pale or yellowing lower leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig can point to too little light or a nutrient shortage during active growth. Wipe the broad leaves of the Fiddle-leaf fig with a damp cloth now and then to clear dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and scale. Steady light, steady watering, and stable temperature prevent most Fiddle-leaf fig problems.

Water your Fiddle-leaf fig when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in the growing season. Always water the Fiddle-leaf fig thoroughly until liquid drains from the pot, then discard whatever collects in the saucer. Reduce watering for the Fiddle-leaf fig in winter, when the plant uses less moisture and the soil stays damp longer. Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves. Let the moisture level guide your schedule rather than watering on a fixed calendar day.

items.question: How should I water my jade plant in winter compared to summer to avoid overwatering?
items.answer_text: In spring and summer the Jade plant may need water roughly every two to three weeks, while in winter it may need water only once a month. Move the Jade plant outdoors gradually in summer to avoid scorching its leaves. The Jade plant (Crassula ovata) stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings.
cited_quotes: The Jade plant (Crassula ovata) stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water the Jade plant deeply, then let the top two-thirds of the soil dry before watering again. In spring and summer the Jade plant may need water roughly every two to three weeks, while in winter it may need water only once a month. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure with the Jade plant, so err toward keeping it dry. Always empty the saucer so the Jade plant never sits in standing water.

The Jade plant (Crassula ovata) does best in bright light and tolerates several hours of direct sun each day. A south- or west-facing window is a strong choice for the Jade plant indoors. With too little light the Jade plant stretches, grows leggy, and develops weak, spindly stems. Rotate the Jade plant a quarter turn every week or two so it grows evenly toward the light. Move the Jade plant outdoors gradually in summer to avoid scorching its leaves.

items.question: Is a snake plant dangerous if my toddler bites a leaf?
items.answer_text: The strongest growth and the boldest leaf banding on a snake plant appear in bright, indirect light. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a snake plant often follow underwatering or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand.
cited_quotes: Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) adapts to a wide range of light, from bright indirect sun to fairly dim corners. The strongest growth and the boldest leaf banding on a snake plant appear in bright, indirect light. A snake plant kept in deep shade survives but grows slowly and produces thinner leaves. Protect snake plant from prolonged direct midday sun through glass, which can scorch and bleach the leaves. Rotating the snake plant a quarter turn every few weeks keeps its upright leaves growing evenly.

The most frequent problem with snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) is root rot caused by overwatering, which shows as soft, yellowing, or collapsing leaves. Brown, crispy leaf tips on a snake plant often follow underwatering or a buildup of mineral salts from tap water. Wrinkled or curling leaves signal that the snake plant is too dry and needs a thorough watering. Cold drafts below 50 degrees Fahrenheit can leave pale scarred patches on snake plant leaves. If a snake plant is not growing, move it to brighter indirect light and resume regular feeding during the growing season.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata) needs a fast-draining mix, such as a cactus and succulent soil blended with extra perlite or coarse sand. Plant snake plant in a pot with drainage holes, because the rhizomes are prone to rot in waterlogged soil. A snake plant prefers to be slightly root-bound and only needs repotting every three to four years. Repot snake plant in spring, moving it to a container only one size larger. Terracotta pots suit snake plant well because the porous clay wicks away excess moisture.

The Fiddle-leaf fig prefers bright, indirect light and does best near an east- or south-facing window with a sheer curtain. Brown spots on a Fiddle-leaf fig often signal overwatering or root rot, especially when the spots start at the leaf edges and the soil stays wet. Dropped leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig usually follow a sudden change, such as a move, a draft, or a swing in watering. Pale or yellowing lower leaves on the Fiddle-leaf fig can point to too little light or a nutrient shortage during active growth. Wipe the broad leaves of the Fiddle-leaf fig with a damp cloth now and then to clear dust and to check for pests such as spider mites and scale. Steady light, steady watering, and stable temperature prevent most Fiddle-leaf fig problems.

Water your Fiddle-leaf fig when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in the growing season. Always water the Fiddle-leaf fig thoroughly until liquid drains from the pot, then discard whatever collects in the saucer. Reduce watering for the Fiddle-leaf fig in winter, when the plant uses less moisture and the soil stays damp longer. Overwatering is the most common cause of trouble for the Fiddle-leaf fig and can lead to root rot and dropped leaves. Let the moisture level guide your schedule rather than watering on a fixed calendar day.

Soft, mushy, or translucent leaves on an Aloe vera usually signal overwatering and the onset of root rot. Thin, curling leaves instead point to underwatering, so check whether the Aloe vera has gone too long without a drink. Brown, crispy leaf tips on Aloe vera can follow sudden exposure to intense direct sun before the plant has acclimated. A pale, stretched, and floppy Aloe vera is reaching for more light and should be moved gradually to a brighter location. If the base of the Aloe vera turns dark and soft, remove the plant, cut away rotted tissue, and repot it in fresh dry succulent mix.

Aloe vera grows best in bright light and tolerates several hours of direct sun once acclimated. Place Aloe vera near a south- or west-facing window where it receives at least six hours of strong light each day. A plant kept in low light will stretch and grow pale, so move a leggy Aloe vera gradually toward a brighter spot to avoid leaf scorch. If you move Aloe vera outdoors for summer, increase sun exposure slowly over one to two weeks. Leaves that turn reddish-brown often indicate that the Aloe vera is receiving more intense sun than it has adjusted to.

Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) is a succulent that stores water in its leaves and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Water Aloe vera deeply but infrequently, allowing the top two inches of soil to become completely dry first. In spring and summer this usually means watering Aloe vera about every two to three weeks, while in winter the interval often stretches to once a month or less. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure with Aloe vera, so when in doubt, wait a few more days before watering. Always discard any water that collects in the saucer so that the roots of your Aloe vera never sit in moisture.

Aloe vera needs a fast-draining mix, so use a cactus or succulent potting blend amended with extra perlite or coarse sand. Plant Aloe vera in a container with drainage holes, since standing water at the roots quickly leads to rot. Repot Aloe vera every two to three years, or sooner when offsets crowd the pot or roots emerge from the drainage holes. Choose a pot only one size larger, because an oversized container holds excess moisture around the roots of the Aloe vera. After repotting, wait about a week before watering the Aloe vera so that any disturbed roots can heal.

items.question: Is a Calathea safe to keep in a house with cats?
items.answer_text: The cited reference does not list Calathea as toxic to cats or dogs. Keep the Calathea out of reach of young children as a general precaution, since the cited reference addresses pets and not every possible reaction. After repotting, water the Calathea thoroughly and keep it out of direct sun while it settles.
cited_quotes: The cited reference does not list Calathea as toxic to cats or dogs. Households with curious pets often choose the Calathea for this reason, but ingestion of any houseplant can still cause mild stomach upset or vomiting in animals. If your pet eats part of a Calathea and you see concerning symptoms, contact your veterinarian or a poison-control line for guidance. Keep the Calathea out of reach of young children as a general precaution, since the cited reference addresses pets and not every possible reaction.

Pot your Calathea in a light, well-draining mix, such as peat or coir blended with perlite and a little orchid bark. The Calathea likes a container with drainage holes so excess water escapes rather than pooling around the roots. Repot your Calathea every one to two years in spring, moving up just one pot size to refresh the mix and give the roots room. Because the Calathea has fine, shallow roots, handle the root ball gently and avoid packing the soil too tightly. After repotting, water the Calathea thoroughly and keep it out of direct sun while it settles.

Crispy brown leaf edges on a Calathea usually signal low humidity, mineral-heavy water, or letting the soil dry out too far. If the Calathea stops folding its leaves upward at night, it may be receiving too little light or too much stress from inconsistent watering. Spider mites can attack a stressed Calathea, so inspect the undersides of the leaves and rinse them if you spot fine webbing.

Water your Calathea when the top inch of the potting mix has begun to dry, which is often about once every five to seven days in the growing season. Reduce watering for the Calathea in winter to roughly every ten to fourteen days, letting the surface dry slightly more between drinks. Never let the Calathea sit in a saucer of standing water, because soggy roots lead to rot.

The Rubber plant (Ficus elastica) does best in a well-draining potting mix, such as a general houseplant mix amended with perlite or bark. When watering the Rubber plant, water thoroughly until liquid runs from the drainage holes, then discard any water left in the saucer.

The Boston fern thrives in a loose, peat-based or coir-based potting mix that drains freely while holding moisture. Choose a pot for the Boston fern that has drainage holes, since standing water rots its fine roots. Repot the Boston fern every one to two years in spring, moving it up by one pot size when the roots fill the container. When repotting the Boston fern, you can divide a large clump into two or three smaller plants to propagate it. A light monthly feeding with diluted balanced fertilizer during spring and summer keeps the Boston fern lush.

The Boston fern prefers soil that stays evenly and consistently moist but never waterlogged. Water the Boston fern whenever the top half inch of the potting mix begins to feel dry to the touch. In a warm, well-lit room the Boston fern often needs watering two or three times per week, while in winter once every five to seven days is usually enough. Because the Boston fern resents dry air, mist its fronds or set the pot on a humidity tray to keep relative humidity near 50 to 70 percent. The Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) grows best in bright, indirect light for roughly 6 to 8 hours a day. Direct midday sun can scorch the leaves of a Monstera, leaving pale or brown patches, so filter strong light through a sheer curtain. A Monstera kept in deep shade tends to produce smaller leaves with fewer of the characteristic splits and holes. Rotating the Monstera a quarter turn each week helps it grow evenly toward the light source.

The cited reference lists Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) as toxic to cats and dogs; ingestion can cause oral irritation, intense burning of the mouth and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. These effects in the Monstera are caused by insoluble calcium oxalate crystals present throughout the plant's leaves and stems. If a cat or dog chews any part of a Monstera, contact a veterinarian or an animal poison-control line promptly. Keep the Monstera out of reach of pets and children to reduce the chance of accidental ingestion.

Planta la Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) en una mezcla suelta y de buen drenaje, enriquecida con corteza, perlita o fibra de coco para mantener las raíces aireadas. Elige para la Monstera una maceta con orificios de drenaje y solo 2 a 5 centímetros más ancha que el cepellón actual. Trasplanta la Monstera cada 1 a 2 años en primavera, cuando las raíces empiecen a dar vueltas en la maceta o a salir por los orificios de drenaje. Una Monstera madura se beneficia de un tutor de musgo o una estaca, porque sus raíces aéreas trepan y sostienen hojas más grandes y con más fenestraciones.

Plant the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) in a loose, well-draining potting mix amended with bark, perlite, or coir to keep roots aerated. Choose a pot for the Monstera that has drainage holes and is only 2 to 5 centimeters wider than the current root ball. Repot the Monstera every 1 to 2 years in spring when roots begin circling the pot or emerging from the drainage holes. A mature Monstera benefits from a moss pole or stake, because its aerial roots will climb and support larger, more fenestrated leaves.

La Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta durante unas 6 a 8 horas al día. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar las hojas de una Monstera y dejar manchas pálidas o marrones, así que filtra la luz intensa con una cortina fina. Una Monstera mantenida en sombra profunda tiende a producir hojas más pequeñas y con menos de los característicos cortes y agujeros. Girar la Monstera un cuarto de vuelta cada semana le ayuda a crecer de forma uniforme hacia la fuente de luz.

items.question: Es peligroso el lirio de la paz si mi nino muerde una hoja?
items.answer_text: El Lirio de la paz es distinto de los lirios verdaderos del género Lilium, pero igualmente debe tratarse como peligroso para los animales. Las puntas marrones en las hojas del Lirio de la paz suelen indicar poca humedad, acumulación de minerales del agua del grifo o exceso de fertilizante. Las hojas amarillas en el Lirio de la paz normalmente apuntan a un exceso de riego o a raíces que han estado demasiado tiempo en agua.
cited_quotes: El Lirio de la paz es distinto de los lirios verdaderos del género Lilium, pero igualmente debe tratarse como peligroso para los animales.

Las puntas marrones en las hojas del Lirio de la paz suelen indicar poca humedad, acumulación de minerales del agua del grifo o exceso de fertilizante. Las hojas amarillas en el Lirio de la paz normalmente apuntan a un exceso de riego o a raíces que han estado demasiado tiempo en agua. Si el Lirio de la paz se inclina de forma drástica, revisa primero la tierra, ya que tanto la falta de riego como el exceso severo pueden provocar el marchitamiento. Pocas flores o ninguna en el Lirio de la paz suele significar que la luz es demasiado escasa o que la planta es demasiado joven para florecer.

El Lirio de la paz prefiere luz brillante e indirecta y tolera la luz media o baja mejor que la mayoría de las plantas de interior con flor. Mantén el Lirio de la paz lejos del sol directo del mediodía, porque los rayos directos y calientes pueden quemar sus hojas y dejar manchas marrones. Un lugar a un par de metros de una ventana orientada al este o al norte le sienta bien al Lirio de la paz. Con muy poca luz el Lirio de la paz sobrevivirá, pero puede dejar de producir sus espatas blancas. Si las hojas del Lirio de la paz se ven pálidas o alargadas, trasládalo a un sitio más luminoso con luz filtrada.

Planta el Lirio de la paz en un sustrato suelto y con buen drenaje, rico en materia orgánica, como una mezcla a base de turba enmendada con perlita. Elige una maceta con orificios de drenaje, porque el Lirio de la paz no tolera la tierra encharcada. Trasplanta el Lirio de la paz cada uno o dos años en primavera, pasándolo a un recipiente solo una talla más grande. El Lirio de la paz florece de forma más fiable cuando está ligeramente apretado en su maceta, así que evita usar un recipiente demasiado grande. Renueva la capa superior de tierra del Lirio de la paz cada año si no hace falta un trasplante completo.
Limpia de vez en cuando las hojas anchas del Lirio de la paz para quitar el polvo y para revisar si hay plagas como araña roja y cochinillas.

Mantenga la planta ZZ fuera del alcance de mascotas y niños, y lávese las manos después de manipular los tallos cortados o la savia de la planta ZZ. La planta ZZ crece bien con luz indirecta de baja a brillante intensidad, lo que hace de la planta ZZ una opción tolerante para habitaciones poco iluminadas y oficinas. Coloque la planta ZZ cerca de una ventana orientada al este o al norte para recibir luz suave y constante. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar las hojas brillantes, así que mantenga la planta ZZ alejada de los rayos fuertes de la tarde. La planta ZZ crecerá más despacio con muy poca luz, pero aun así sobrevivirá durante meses. Gire la planta ZZ cada pocas semanas para que la planta ZZ crezca de forma pareja hacia la luz.

La planta ZZ almacena agua en sus gruesos rizomas, por lo que la planta ZZ tolera el riego poco frecuente mucho mejor que la mayoría de las plantas de interior. Riegue la planta ZZ solo cuando las 2 pulgadas superiores del sustrato se hayan secado por completo, lo que suele significar cada dos o tres semanas. En invierno la planta ZZ necesita aún menos, y regar una vez al mes suele ser suficiente para la planta ZZ. El exceso de riego es la forma más común de dañar una planta ZZ, porque el sustrato encharcado pudre los rizomas. En caso de duda, deje seca la planta ZZ en lugar de tomar la regadera.

Place the ZZ plant near an east- or north-facing window for steady, gentle light. Direct midday sun can scorch the glossy leaves, so keep the ZZ plant out of harsh afternoon rays. The ZZ plant will grow more slowly in very low light but will still survive for months. Rotate the ZZ plant every few weeks so the ZZ plant grows evenly toward the light.

La planta ZZ necesita un sustrato con buen drenaje, y una mezcla preparada para cactus o suculentas le conviene bien a la planta ZZ. Plante siempre la planta ZZ en un recipiente con orificios de drenaje para que el exceso de agua pueda salir de los rizomas. Las arañas rojas son la plaga más común en la hiedra (Hedera helix), especialmente en aire interior cálido y seco. Los bordes de las hojas marrones y quebradizos en la hiedra suelen indicar baja humedad o riego irregular. Las hojas amarillas en la hiedra a menudo apuntan a un exceso de riego o a un drenaje deficiente en las raíces. Los tallos alargados y ralos en la hiedra indican luz insuficiente, así que traslada la planta a un lugar más luminoso. Rocía la hiedra o agrúpala con otras plantas para aumentar la humedad y desalentar a las arañas rojas.

La hiedra (Hedera helix) crece bien en un sustrato a base de turba con buen drenaje y enmendado con perlita para mejorar la aireación. Elige para la hiedra una maceta con orificios de drenaje para evitar que el agua se acumule en las raíces. Trasplanta la hiedra cada uno o dos años en primavera, aumentando solo un tamaño de maceta a la vez. La hiedra prefiere un cepellón ligeramente ajustado y puede resentirse si se le da un recipiente demasiado grande. Renueva la capa superior del sustrato anualmente para la hiedra cuando no sea necesario un trasplante completo.

La hiedra (Hedera helix) crece mejor con luz brillante e indirecta cerca de una ventana orientada al este o al norte. La hiedra tolera la luz media, pero producirá un crecimiento ralo y alargado en sombra profunda. Las formas variegadas de la hiedra necesitan más luz indirecta para conservar sus marcas color crema y blanco. El sol directo del mediodía puede quemar las hojas de la hiedra, así que filtra la luz fuerte con una cortina translúcida. Gira la hiedra un cuarto de vuelta cada semana para que el crecimiento sea parejo en todos los lados.

La hiedra (Hedera helix) prefiere un sustrato uniformemente húmedo que se deje secar ligeramente entre riegos. Riega la hiedra cuando la primera pulgada del sustrato se sienta seca al tacto, lo que suele ocurrir aproximadamente una vez cada cinco a siete días en crecimiento activo. En invierno, reduce el riego de la hiedra a aproximadamente una vez cada diez a catorce días, ya que el crecimiento se ralentiza. La hiedra es sensible a las raíces encharcadas, así que vacía el plato después de regar y nunca dejes la maceta sobre agua estancada. El exceso de riego de la hiedra es una causa de deterioro más común que la falta de agua.

English ivy (Hedera helix) prefers evenly moist soil that is allowed to dry slightly between waterings. Water English ivy when the top inch of soil feels dry to the touch, which is often about once every five to seven days in active growth. In winter, reduce watering for English ivy to roughly once every ten to fourteen days as growth slows. English ivy is sensitive to soggy roots, so empty the saucer after watering and never leave the pot standing in water. Overwatering English ivy is a more common cause of decline than underwatering.
